Benjamin Franklin mocked the bald eagle in a 1784 letter and praised the turkey, but never asked for it to be the national bird

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1066 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The letter, never mailed to his daughter, was not published in full in English until 1817.
  • A popular Thanksgiving story holds that Benjamin Franklin wanted the turkey, not the bald eagle, to be the national bird of the United States.
  • The story traces back to a letter dated January 26, 1784, and addressed to his daughter, Sarah Bache.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The letter, never mailed to his daughter, was not published in full in English until 1817. The bald eagle became the national bird by law only in 2024.

A popular Thanksgiving story holds that Benjamin Franklin wanted the turkey, not the bald eagle, to be the national bird of the United States. It is a good story, but it is not what Franklin actually wrote.

The story traces back to a letter dated January 26, 1784, and addressed to his daughter, Sarah Bache. In it, he poked fun at the eagle on the badge of the Society of the Cincinnati and said a few kind words about the turkey. In that letter, he never proposes the turkey as a national symbol.

According to the editors of his papers, Franklin never even sent the letter to his daughter. And the bald eagle itself was officially designated the national bird by law only in 2024, more than two centuries later.

Recent findings suggest that when Franklin wrote the letter, the bald eagle was already on the Great Seal of the United States. It had been adopted for the seal on June 20, 1782.

In the winter of 1783 to 1784, Franklin, the American minister, was too ill to travel and isolated at Passy, in France, according to the editors of his papers.

Sources indicate that on January 26, he saw the founding document of the Society of the Cincinnati, a hereditary order of American army officers. John Paul Jones had sent it to him along with a pamphlet attacking the society.

The letter that Franklin wrote that same day was, in the view of the editors of The Papers of Benjamin Franklin, a satire meant as a public essay.

Addressing it to his daughter, with whom, the editors note, he never corresponded about politics, made it look like a private note.

In a recent development, he took aim at the idea of passing honors down to children. He objected to “an order of hereditary Knights, in direct opposition to the solemnly declared sense of their country.”.

Recent findings suggest that he even did the math. In nine generations, he wrote, a member’s share in his descendant would be “but a 512th part.”.

Industry observers note that the birds come up near the end, when Franklin turns to the society’s badges, which had been made in France. “To me they seem tolerably done; but all such things are criticised,” he wrote.

Some critics, he reported, disliked the Latin mottos. “Others object to the bald eagle, as looking too much like a Dindon or turkey,” he wrote, using the French word for turkey.

Industry observers note that then Franklin gave his own opinion. “For my own part I wish the bald eagle had not been chosen as the representative of our country,” he wrote. “He is a bird of bad moral character. He does not get his living honestly.”.

It has been revealed that he described the eagle sitting on a dead tree, “too lazy to fish for himself,” while it watched another bird, which he called the fishing hawk. When that bird caught a fish and carried it toward its nest, he wrote, the eagle “pursues him, and takes it from him.”.

According to recent reports, he went further. “Besides he is a rank coward,” Franklin wrote. The “little king bird not bigger than a sparrow attacks him boldly and drives him out of the district.”.

Recent findings suggest that only then does Franklin praise the turkey. He wrote that he was “not displeased” that the figure on the badge was not recognizable as a bald eagle and looked more like a turkey.

“For in truth, the turkey is in comparison a much more respectable bird, and withal a true original native of America,” he wrote. Eagles, he noted, “have been found in all countries, but the turkey was peculiar to ours.”.

He did not spare the turkey entirely. He called it “a little vain and silly,” though “not the worse emblem for that,” and “a bird of courage” that would attack a grenadier of the British guards who dared to invade its farmyard “with a red coat on.”.

Industry observers note that nowhere in the letter does Franklin ask for the turkey to replace the eagle on the seal or anywhere else. The comparison is part of a joke about a badge.

According to the editors of his papers, Franklin demonstrated the letter only to his grandsons before sending it, around March 1784, to the abbé Morellet in France to translate it into French. Morellet advised against publishing it. Franklin agreed and promised it would not appear while he was alive.

A partial French translation came out in Paris in 1790, months after Franklin’s death. The full English text was not published until 1817, when William Temple Franklin included it in his edition of Franklin’s writings.

In other words, the letter that so many people now quote was almost unknown in Franklin’s lifetime.

The bald eagle’s official title came with a bill that Sen. Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota introduced on June 20, 2024, exactly 242 years after the eagle was adopted for the Great Seal.

According to recent reports, the Senate passed it by unanimous consent in July 2024, and the House approved it by voice vote on December 16, 2024. It was signed into law on December 23, 2024, as Public Law 118-206.

The law adds a new section to the U.S. Code. It reads: “The bald eagle (Haliaeetus leucocephalus) is the national bird.”.

In its findings, Congress noted that the bald eagle is unique to North America and that federal, state and local governments, nonprofit groups and individuals had all contributed to its recovery.

Even so, eagles still face problems, including the lead poisoning that is common in eagles.

The turkey’s history with people goes back much further than Franklin. Scientists have found that turkeys were domesticated at least 1,500 years ago.

In a recent development, the information was obtained from Benjamin Franklin’s letter to Sarah Bache of January 26, 1784, as published by the National Archives in Founders Online from The Papers of Benjamin Franklin, the record of S.4610 on Congress.gov, and the enrolled text of the bill published by the U.S. Government Publishing Office.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Sebnem Ece Eksi did a double take. Proteins typically studied in the brain were turning up in prostate cancer cells from high-risk patients. These proteins, called neuronal adhesion molecules, play a key role in the circuitry associated with memory.

The finding, made during her Ph.D. days at the University of Illinois Chicago, raised so many questions to which Eksi is still seeking answers. Now at the Oregon Health & Science University in Portland, Eksi has made it her lab’s goal to find out how nervous systems communicate with cancer. What were once two separate fields might be connected more closely than previously thought.

Sources indicate that “What we’re learning is that tumors are actively communicating with the nervous system,” Eksi says. “In a way, it makes sense to me that a growing tumor in our bodies, in an organ, would be immediately sensed and detected by the nervous system.”.

Eksi now aims to test an AI image-based recognition algorithm to identify nerve fibers in human patients. This is exciting, she claims, because these nerves aren’t normally visible in patient tumors. But through biopsies, she hopes to map out and observe how the nervous system — which impacts sleep, cognition and pain — changes as cancer progresses. The implications are significant, she says. Could experts use the nervous system to detect cancer early? Can they improve patients’ quality of life?

“This field of cancer neuroscience can change all different stages of cancer diagnosis and treatments,” Eksi notes. “It’s growing so rapidly, the field itself.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that the campaign of Mississippi’s Sen.-elect Scott Colom was rightfully praised for its clever and brutal ads.
  • It has been revealed that however, it was fitting that the Democrat’s closing message traded the edge for a solemn reminder of who and what brought him so far on his journey to his election as Mississippi’s first Black U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, sen.-elect Scott Colom speaks during a victory rally at Tougaloo College on Nov. 11. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images).

Recent findings suggest that the campaign of Mississippi’s Sen.-elect Scott Colom was rightfully praised for its clever and brutal ads. The “pick another protein” spot will forever be stuck in the brains of a huge swath of Americans, especially Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith. She underestimated Colom and his team, and will soon be an ex-senator.

It has been revealed that however, it was fitting that the Democrat’s closing message traded the edge for a solemn reminder of who and what brought him so far on his journey to his election as Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction.

The ad delivered an all-American lesson about history, born of bravery and sacrifice.

Filmed at the Jackson, Miss., home of slain civil rights leader Medgar Evers, the ad featured Colom recounting the story of Evers, a World War II veteran who survived Normandy, only to be shot in the back by a racist assassin, resentful that a Black man dared to exercise his rights as a citizen in the country he fought for.

“He was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” Colom said. “On Tuesday, use your vote and honor everyone who died for that right.”.

In a state where voting is still racially polarized, it was clear that Colom would not win over a majority of white voters; he won an estimated 25 percent, better than Democrats in recent elections and cutting into Trump’s margins, but certainly not a path to victory.

Black voters in Mississippi made the difference, as they often have. With their allies in the cause of justice, they heeded the call. They indicated up despite the state’s stringent and often confusing voting restrictions, purges of the voting rolls engineered by Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson (who used unverified data from a credit bureau), and the U.S. Supreme Court Louisiana v. Callais decision that led to a wave of Southern states breaking up Black-majority districts.

When the Mississippi purges resulted in “affidavit ballots” that required verification to count, as The Washington Post reported, young Black women tracked down those voters, one by one, to do everything they could to ensure voters’ efforts were not in vain.

Black voters mattered in states all over the country, but especially in the South, where low turnout has plagued Democrats, particularly in midterm elections.

Sources indicate that keisha Lance Bottoms was elected the first Black female governor in the country in Georgia, where Democrats won up and down the ballot. Newly elected senators Annie Andrews in South Carolina and James Talarico of Texas campaigned for and earned support from Black voters with proposals that rose above platitudes. And don’t sleep on North Carolina, where voters flipped seats the GOP tried to gerrymander into a hardened majority. The sight of hundreds of students from HBCU NC A&T State University, denied a campus early voting site, marching to the polls, must have made the ancestors smile.

In Florida and Louisiana, where Democrats had little financial support and lost their statewide races, Black voters brought them tantalizingly close to victory and energized for the contests to come.

I still don’t expect Republicans to give up the election shenanigans, done in the name of “election integrity” and color blindness but in reality designed to demoralize as much as suppress. Why try to win over a diverse electorate with an inclusive, policy-driven message when manipulating Black-majority districts can still work?

Recent findings suggest that the number of Black U.S. House members in the next session of Congress will fall, offset by a few Democrats who survived in redrawn districts, including Shomari Figures of Alabama and Don Davis of North Carolina.

But you can’t redistrict a state, and you can’t skip town halls and expect tradition, support for the Confederacy and an “R” after your name to forever save you — the Hyde-Smith playbook.

"I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge, and you blocked him from being U.S. senator," she bragged, too soon, on election night.

Maybe she should have emphasized affordability, saving rural hospitals and serving all Mississippians, as Colom did.

What did GOP officials in those Southern red states think they would accomplish by focusing on their base and ignoring everyone else in states they were supposed to be serving?

Did they not pay attention in history class, or maybe they attended one of those post-integration private schools where an unedited version of America’s past might not have been on the lesson initiative?

Did they believe that voters who remembered Evers, Fannie Lou Hamer, Vernon Dahmer and countless others would shrug and say “you win” when legislatures and elections officials quickly and cynically pounced to quiet their voices?

That would be disrespectful to all the people who worked for, sometimes died for rights they knew they may never enjoy, yet had a belief in America and the rightness of their cause.

It has been revealed that scott Colom and the Evers family remembered. He was emotional in his reaction, in an MS NOW interview, when asked about the statement from Reena Evers-Everette, daughter of Medgar and Myrlie Evers. “Their courage helped make this moment possible,” she said.

Colum agreed: “I absolutely stand on their shoulders. And from the bottom of my heart, I’m going to do everything I can to make them proud.”.

Post-election, he has been very gracious, saying that he intends to serve all Mississippians, including the woman whom I suspect would hit a different note if the election had turned in her favor.

Industry observers note that I have no doubt Scott Colom means it. He knows who paid the price to get him this far.

According to recent reports, yian Yin seeks to understand the dynamics of science itself. The computational social scientist is particularly interested in how innovations happen and how they may be accelerated.

“I want to understand what the secret sources or recipes of success are,” says Yin, of Cornell University.

Sources indicate that he applied machine learning techniques to accepted and rejected research proposals to understand how scientists learn from failures. What he found was that scientists fail, and they fail often. Some switched gears after some rejections, but others who continued their research and incorporated feedback found success at a faster rate. Those who changed ideas or scrapped original proposals did not leverage a lot from their experience.

“A group that’s not only failing better and better,” Yin states, “is also failing faster and increasingly faster towards their eventual success.”.

More recently, Yin has been investigating how generative AI is changing scientific publishing. Journals are receiving more AI-assisted submissions than ever before, which is leading the peer-review process to falter. More seemingly well-written papers that lack substance are getting through, he found. Coming up with large-scale solutions requires looking at the issue in a measurable way, Yin says.

“Considering both the technological and social side of scientific ecosystems would be something that’s really beneficial for the ongoing public debate and discussion about how we accelerate science in the age of artificial intelligence,” Yin claims.

In a recent development, rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., speaks during a news conference at the Capitol last summer. Few details have emerged so far about the government’s search of her home earlier this fall. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

It has been revealed that A judge noted he will order the release of some information about the federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., which included a search of her Washington house last month.

Judge James Boasberg for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia made the statement Tuesday during a hearing brought by news organizations and an advocacy group seeking details about the search. Boasberg ordered the government to provide him by Friday what could be disclosed in the case. He pointed to how investigators are handling the “speech or debate” clause immunity that Omar has as a sitting member of Congress.

“This is purely legal questions, interesting questions, about the privilege, the extent of the privilege and how it would apply,” Boasberg noted.

The Constitution includes an immunity for members of Congress for the “speech or debate” they engage in as part of their jobs.

According to recent reports, boasberg also directed the government to propose redactions to the as-yet secret docket. While he remarked next week’s expected disclosures would not include the 67-page document that investigators provided to justify the search, he left the door open to unsealing that down the road if the government closes the case or brings charges.

Justice Department attorney Alessandra Serano argued against broad disclosures, calling it “very rare that a precharging, pre-indictment unsealing would happen.”.

The high-profile nature of the investigation leaked into the courtroom Tuesday, as Boasberg cited statements by President Donald Trump and others about the investigation into Omar.

“You have had administration officials, prominent ones, talking about the purpose of the investigation,” Boasberg noted.

Administration officials have accused Omar of committing immigration crimes for years, and Trump said last month the DOJ was looking into Omar “strongly.” Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on a recent podcast that investigators had served multiple search warrants and were investigating possible immigration fraud tied to when Omar entered the United States as a child.

Separately, Boasberg said he may issue rulings in the coming weeks unsealing portions of other court cases tied to the investigation, including one brought by Omar herself earlier this month seeking the return of the items seized in the search.

The administration executed the search warrant in October, just a few weeks before the midterm elections. The timing of the search drew accusations of political bias from Democrats who claimed that the administration brought the case to sway the midterm elections.

For years Trump has said he wanted criminal charges to be brought against his political foes, including Omar and others in Congress.

In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Industry observers note that in an increasingly fire-prone western North America, Jennifer Grenz, an ecologist and member of the Lytton First Nation, looks at fire with a holistic eye. She considers her work with landscapes recovering from catastrophic wildfire to be “deliberately unfocused,” spanning soil microbial ecology, restoration ecology, invasion biology and historical biology.

Grenz analyzes historical ecological records, like how Indigenous people have shaped and cared for ecosystems over time, to paint a comprehensive picture. “I’m interested in how those histories leave ecological legacies and hints of the stewardship of the past,” claims Grenz, who leads the Indigenous Ecology Lab at the University of British Columbia in Canada. “What changed on the land that made it more vulnerable?”.

Grenz spends time with many kinds of specialists, such as archaeologists, anthropologists and Indigenous elders who provide oral histories.

Moving forward, her lab will examine ecology below ground, including soil, microbial communities and root networks. The goal is to understand the role of underground ecology in critical topics like carbon sequestration, climate change, biodiversity and sustainable management.

Recent findings suggest that “My motivation is in our interior Salish Territories in the southern interior of British Columbia, where my ancestors rest and where my people are,” Grenz says. “The responsibility I feel to them and to our Tmícw, which means our lands, [is] to not take us back to the past, but to show that we have the deep knowledge to help us move forward.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

It has been revealed that dor Minzer remembers sitting in an undergraduate computation class at Tel Aviv University. He was intrigued by his professor and soon found himself pulled into a new world: the mystifying intersection of math and computation, first laid out by Alan Turing during World War II. Working with the professor, Minzer became deeply interested in the limitations of what computers can and can’t do.

In a recent development, “My part is actually to prove not only do I not know how to do it, but I can prove that it’s impossible,” Minzer says. “You have to really be curious.”.

It has been revealed that minzer’s hard work has paid off. In 2018, he proved a theoretical computer science problem called the 2-to-2 games conjecture. It asks whether computers can efficiently distinguish games where almost all rules can be satisfied from those where almost none can be satisfied, when the rules have a strict structure.

Sources indicate that in September, Minzer and his two graduate students at MIT posted a 95-page milestone paper on the unique games conjecture, which builds off the 2-to-2 conjecture. The paper wasn’t quite ready, but they published to get ahead of a press release from OpenAI, describing its proof for the same problem, slated for only days later. It’s a situation that many mathematicians have found themselves in this year as AI companies flood the field with findings at lightning speed.

In a recent development, minzer notes it’s critical to remember that math, and all the research and contemplation behind it, is very human. “It’s a human activity,” he says. “Research is sort of a living organism, a living body.”.

Recent findings suggest that minzer teaches his own students now. Some days, he talks to his class and gets the sense that nobody is paying attention. But other days, he gets a few students that participate. They have ideas, they’re excited, and they remind him of his own days as a graduate student.

Industry observers note that choose toys that allow your kid to use their imagination and play out multiple different situations, both real and made up. Furthermore, make sure even if you want the toy to help them learn STEM skills, it still fits their interests and passions. Industry observers note that isabel Angelo spends her days searching the cosmos for exoplanets and signs of extraterrestrial intelligence. But Angelo’s head isn’t in the stars. It’s buried under mountains of 0s and 1s — data from space telescopes old and new.

To piece together a fuller picture of what’s out there (alien megastructures around nearby stars, perhaps?), Angelo and her colleagues at the SETI Institute in Mountain View, Calif., are turning to machine learning models. These tools are analyzing the troves of telescope data for anomalies — things that look “weird” in space that we don’t know how to explain yet.

Industry observers note that most of the space weirdos will probably turn out to be total normies — a comet, a newborn star or a star surrounded by lots of gas and dust. “These are things that I would expect [the models] to find,” Angelo says. “But the goal is to find something that’s not even in any of these categories.”.

Recent findings suggest that in the meantime, Angelo keeps her whimsy and wonder for space alive by remembering historic moments, like the reveal of the first portrait of a black hole in 2019. The scientists “put all of these telescopes all over the Earth. They wait for the Earth to rotate. They do all this math to construct this one image,” Angelo says. “I can’t believe how creative and innovative we have to be to learn about space. It’s such a specific and really fun challenge.”.

  • Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

According to recent reports, in 1985, the W.M. Keck Foundation donated $70 million for the University of California and Caltech to construct a new observatory on Maunakea in Hawaii. The twin telescopes of the Keck Observatory would be larger than any previous telescope, and the first to use a segmented-mirror design. The goal was a facility that could see farther out into the universe, and with more detail, to study exoplanets, black holes, star and planet formation, and more.

Sources indicate that on Nov. 24, 1990, with only nine of the 36 segments of its mirror in place, Keck I turned skyward and achieved first light. The telescope’s image of NGC 1232 was an auspicious beginning of a long career for the Keck Observatory, furthered when Keck I was completed in 1992, and when Keck II was constructed and saw first light in October 1996. The twin telescopes would become the most scientifically productive optical and infrared telescopes in the world.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

If you’ve been waiting to find a great deal on emergency backup power for your home or portable power for a road trip, Black Friday and Cyber Monday are some of the best times to find the lowest prices on home generators, portable generators, power stations, and solar generators. The good news is that deals are already dropping, even before the holiday shopping season.

According to recent reports, this year, Black Friday falls on November 27, and you can expect discounts as high as 40 percent or more, with prices as low as, or sometimes even better than, what you can expect to find on Prime Day. If you’ve been waiting for a good deal on backup power for your home or even just a few devices, this is a great time to buy.

Start by considering what you want to power during an emergency, like a refrigerator, a computer setup, or the entire house. Or, if you're camping or on a job site, consider the devices you want to power or recharge, such as power tools or camping gear like portable refrigerators.

It has been revealed that then consider the type of generator or power station you want. Fuel-based generators can run as long as you have enough fuel, but they’re loud and must be run outside because they emit potentially dangerous fumes. Power stations, on the other hand, run virtually silently and don’t emit fumes, so you can run them inside, making them great for city dwellers. They need to be recharged, but you can do that with AC power or a solar panel.

No matter what type you choose, it will cost several hundred dollars or more, so Black Friday and Cyber Monday are a good time to knock 20 to 40 percent off the regular price, including popular brands such as Jackery, Bluetti, EcoFlow, Generac, and Champion Power Equipment.

So, if you already have a station you love, you can extend its runtime with a deal on an expansion battery.

Buying a station and panels together is usually a good way to save money, especially on Black Friday, when these bundles go on sale for some of the lowest prices.

Tried and true, fuel-powered generators are popular because they can run indefinitely, as long as you have enough fuel on hand. Some run on just gasoline, while dual- or tri-fuel generators add propane or natural gas as alternatives. They can be loud, so an inverter generator reduces noise pollution and delivers cleaner power that’s safe for sensitive electronics like TVs. Black Friday discounts on generators aren’t typically as deep as those on power stations, but you can still find deals of 10 to 40 percent off.

Motion under the ocean explains the depth of the world’s deepest spot

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Challenger Deep is the deepest valley in the deepest trench in the ocean, plunging to roughly 11,000 meters below sea level.
  • Now, scientists have a new clue about how it got to be so … well, deep.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Challenger Deep is the deepest valley in the deepest trench in the ocean, plunging to roughly 11,000 meters below sea level.

Now, scientists have a new clue about how it got to be so … well, deep.

Industry observers note that challenger Deep is found within the Mariana Trench, a crescent-shaped gouge in the seafloor east of the Philippines in the Pacific Ocean. The trench is the scene of a slo-mo tectonic collision called a subduction zone: The Pacific plate is diving beneath the Mariana plate, bending downward as it sinks into the mantle, forming a steep trench on the ocean floor.

All subduction zones are deep, but “it’s interesting why this is the deepest spot in the Earth’s ocean,” states geoscientist Robert Stern, an emeritus professor at the University of Texas at Dallas and a visiting researcher at the University of California, Los Angeles.

He and colleagues employed a remotely operated robot called ROV Jason/Medea to descend to more than 6,000 meters and explore the Mariana Trench seafloor around the edges of Challenger Deep. The rocks turned out to contain pyroclastic deposits, evidence of an erstwhile explosive volcanic eruption. Those deposits included platelike blocks that could indicate eruption pulses, and lobe-shaped rocks where the volcanic flows ended and quickly cooled.

These are the deepest pyroclastic deposits found on Earth, the scientists report November 23 in Frontiers in Earth Science.

Recent findings suggest that how explosive an eruption is at Earth’s surface depends on the chemical makeup of the magma. When the molten rock contains a high proportion of volatile gases, including water vapor, those gases suddenly expand when the magma reaches the surface, producing a violent explosion.

According to recent reports, such explosive volcanism shouldn’t be possible in the deep sea; the pressure is too high for any escaping gases to expand, Stern states. Along with that mystery, the volcanic deposits were found unusually close to the trench, compared with what would be expected for a subduction zone.

Stern and his colleagues developed a hypothesis that incorporates these disparate pieces of evidence: The extreme depth of Challenger Deep, they say, may be at least partially due to an especially sharp bend in the Pacific Plate as it sinks into the mantle.

It has been revealed that that tighter bend would explain why volcanism is happening closer to the subduction zone than usual. The classic subduction zone scenario is that the sinking plate heats up and melts partially as it descends; the magma rises through the overhanging plate and erupts, forming volcanic island arcs several hundred kilometers from the collision zone. Here, the volcanic deposits were just a hundred kilometers or so from the trench — which makes sense if the plate is dipping more steeply.

As for the pyroclastics, “we can’t answer if the eruptions were really explosive,” Stern notes. But at those pressures, any gases such as water vapor contained in the magma wouldn’t be able to explosively expand as they would at the surface.

According to recent reports, instead, the pyroclastic rocks might have formed through a new version of deep-sea eruption, one in which water emerging from the magma is initially in a supercritical fluid state. That would minimize any explosive expansion during the eruption and could also produce fragmented, dense deposits like those seen by Jason/Medea.

Sources indicate that the discovery of deep-sea pyroclastics is “surprising and unprecedented,” says William Chadwick, a geologist at Oregon State University in Newport. Challenger Deep may be the only place on Earth “with the ingredients to produce explosive volcanism in the super-deep ocean,” he says. “Imagining this happening is … pretty mind-boggling.”.

Recent findings suggest that A lot more work remains to be done to evaluate all of these new ideas, Stern says. “But a lot of things are now coming together.”.

The 6 Best Portable Generators Give You Power Whenever and Wherever You Need It

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • According to recent reports, generators come in all sizes, but when you need power for camping or tailgating, or to power tools when you’re too far from an outlet, a large one meant for home backup is just too much.
  • Recent findings suggest that when you’re shopping for a portable generator, there are a few crucial things to consider, including power, weight, and fuel type.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

According to recent reports, generators come in all sizes, but when you need power for camping or tailgating, or to power tools when you’re too far from an outlet, a large one meant for home backup is just too much. Power stations are handy, but once they run out of power, they take a long time to recharge. That’s where a smaller-sized portable generator can really shine. So long as you have the fuel, they can keep running.

Recent findings suggest that when you’re shopping for a portable generator, there are a few crucial things to consider, including power, weight, and fuel type. For portable power, models that output 2,000 to 5,000 watts will generally be simple enough to lift in and out of a truck, though some models that generate more are designed to be lightweight. Anything over 100 pounds starts to buck the idea of something being portable, even if it has wheels.

Fuel type matters, too. All generators run on gas, but dual-fuel models can also run on propane. The drawback is that propane delivers slightly less power output and shorter running time, but it runs a lot cleaner and is much less messy to deal with.

It has been revealed that if you’re powering sensitive electronics like digital equipment or TVs, you’ll also want to look for an inverter generator, which delivers more stable “cleaner” power that won’t damage your gear. They also run quieter than standard models. For these reasons, all of the picks on our list are inverter generators.

It has been revealed that keeping portability in mind, the models we cover in this story are all 7,500 watts and under. For the models that we tested, we based our methods on our experience using generators for backup power with and without transfer switches, on construction sites to run power tools and equipment, as well as running sound systems and lighting at outdoor events. We measured the sound levels of these generators idling with no load, and while running under load at two feet and 25 feet. We then used an oscilloscope to observe the sine wave of the alternating current generated by these machines, and a clamp meter to check voltage output.

Some examples of devices we used with large starting and running loads include a large air conditioner and a portable table saw. In one case, we even tested it paired to a solar inverter-charger. We evaluated these generators based on ease of starting, power response, sound levels, value, safety, and reliability to select the top performers.

It has been revealed that the Honda EU2200i inverter generator has just about everything you want from a portable generator. It’s half the size and weight of comparable generators in its class; it’s very quiet and clean when operating; and it’s fully enclosed so you can quickly and easily transport it and move it around without worrying about it getting caught on anything.

That enclosure is an important feature, as it protects the inverter electronics and helps contain noise—the EU2200i is remarkably quiet. In testing, we measured sound levels of 68.9 decibels at the generator under no load. When we switched it to “eco” mode, which reduces engine speed when power isn’t called for, the sound was reduced to 76 decibels.

According to recent reports, when we used an oscilloscope to look at the sine wave of the current generated, the curves were smooth and symmetrical, an indicator of “clean” power. This remained true even when running heavy loads from devices like a table saw or an air conditioner.

In a recent development, there are some nice design features, too. The vent on the gas cap closes so fumes or fuel cannot escape. You could breathe freely packing this in the passenger compartment of an SUV. Likewise, the power on/off switch doubles as a fuel shutoff, so it can’t be forgotten.

Lastly, the EU2200i has ports for parallel operation. With the correct cable kit, it connects to a second EU2200i to double the output to 4,400 starting and 3,600 running watts. The EU2200i is ideal for camping and other outdoor events where generator noise might be frowned on.

We like the GD400BN because it’s powerful, quiet, and portable at a reasonable price point. The interesting thing about this inverter generator is how much power it can deliver, yet it’s still as compact as similar generators that deliver half as much output. Even when running on lower-output propane as the fuel source, it can run up to 3,000 watts, which is considerable for a generator that only weighs 47 pounds.

Industry observers note that another plug or two would’ve been nice, however. Its single AC outlet limits you to plugging one power tool or appliance at a time, despite having enough output to power more than one device. It does have a 120-volt, 30-amp outlet for connecting to an RV, though, so that does make up for it a bit, but only if you have that need. The 1.1-gallon fuel tank is also a bit limiting regarding runtime for gasoline, but that’s easily overcome by using propane. For all intents and purposes, this is a very nice dual-fuel generator, and at a list price of $600, it comes at a reasonable price to boot.

The Wen DF360iX offers a considerable amount of utility for an affordable price. You have the option to run the generator on gasoline or propane with a running output of up to 2,900 watts. While propane delivers a bit less at 2,600 watts, that’s plenty of power for a job site or camping use and even enough electricity for small to midsize RVs.

While this generator is fairly light at 49 pounds, it doesn’t cut back on ports, including a 30-amp port for direct connection to an RV. There are also two three-prong AC ports, a 12-volt DC receptacle, and two USB-A ports. Like most inverter generators, it produces less noise. This model is rated at around 65 decibels of noise at a quarter load, which is quiet enough that it shouldn’t bother the neighbors. There are some nice safety features, too, including auto-shutoff if the fuel runs too low and a carbon monoxide (CO) sensor that detects if dangerous levels are present.

Of course, with any generator in this price range (under $500), there are compromises. This model has a pretty small fuel tank—only 1.5 gallons—so you won’t be able to run this on gasoline for long periods (around five hours with a half-load) without having to stop and refill. You can mitigate this, however, by relying on a larger tank of propane. For example, a 20-pound tank should enable you to run it for up to 14 hours.

In a recent development, GENERATOR SAFETYWhile not hard to run, generators present dangers, so you need to follow basic safety rules. Never operate them in a closed space, like a garage or shed. Exhaust gases contain carbon monoxide (CO), a lethal, odorless, colorless gas. Most manufacturers offer models that shut down when they detect carbon monoxide building up. Do not run a generator in a garage with the door open, or in front of the garage with the door open, because carbon monoxide can still get trapped and seep into the house. Run generators at least 20 feet away, including from windows and doors, with the exhaust blowing away from the house.

According to recent reports, RV owners need a generator outfitted with at least a 120-volt, 30-amp outlet, but it also helps to have a decent amount of power to go with it, so that you can run things like a heater or an air conditioner. This model from Champion offers both, with the outlet and up to 3,500 running watts, which is enough to power a small- to medium-sized RV.

It also offers great fuel flexibility. With a full 2.3-gallon fuel tank, it should be able to run for up to 14 hours, but it’s dual-fuel, so with a full 20-pound propane tank, this generator can supply 21 hours of uninterrupted power.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to being a solid companion for camping and RVing, this generator could serve as a useful tool in an emergency at home where power is needed. Using a manual transfer switch, you could power a few 120-volt circuits using the 30-amp connection. And the inverter will help to keep it running more quietly, which is helpful at home or the campground.

One of our test editors picked up this generator when faced with a home emergency where he needed a generator with specific features, swiftly, and on a budget. A failed generator at a solar-powered off-grid cabin necessitated the quick acquisition, and, happily, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel Inverter Generator revealed up on the doorstep in only two days.

It has been revealed that in about 15 minutes, with minimal assembly and after adding oil, the generator was connected to a propane cylinder by a hose and was running on the first cycle of the starter. Since then, it’s run steadily at 500 watts, up to 5,500 watts, at 240 volts (great for powering high-voltage appliances like dryers or water pumps), to charge a battery bank during the winter when sunlight wasn’t enough to get the job done.

This Pulsar puts out very clean power, too, with a claimed total harmonic distortion (THD) of less than 3 percent, which met the requirements of the solar inverter-charger it was paired with.

It has been revealed that using the inverter to monitor the current frequency, we found that it was indeed very stable with minimal variance, between 59.97 and 60.09 Hz. All things considered, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel is a good value for the specs, capacity, and features.

Generac’s iQ3800 Portable Inverter Generator is a great example of what we love about dual-fuel, inverter generators. This type of generator can deliver cleaner power than a standard model, meaning there’s less distortion in the electrical current frequency. That’s ideal for powering sensitive electronics, such as TVs, computer equipment, and smart household appliances. This is also a closed-frame inverter generator, which tends to be quieter; the iQ3800 is one of the quietest generators we’ve tested of this size.

We were very impressed with how easy the iQ3800 is to operate. The electric start and auto choke worked perfectly, taking only about four to five seconds, while the manual pull-start also fired up the generator with minimal effort. Switching between fuel types was also very simple to perform. Once running, you can view notable information on an easy-to-read LED display that lists the total hours the machine has run, the fuel level for the gasoline tank (there’s no gauge for propane), and a load gauge that uses a bar graph to show power output level—knowing that helps to avoid overloading the generator.

Industry observers note that the inverter technology might be the most vital feature of the iQ3800. This generator has a total harmonic distortion (THD)—a level of variance in the current frequency—of less than 3 percent, which is very low. Essentially, anything with a screen or any smart device would be best powered using an inverter generator like the iQ3800. It’s an ideal generator to power RVs in campgrounds or off-grid, and a great option for emergency backup in urban areas.

Full Generac iQ3800 Portable Inverter Generator Review.

It has been revealed that these generators, sometimes called backup generators, are used to provide temporary power when and where it is needed. Portable is a relative term; some are more portable than others. While the smallest models can be picked up and carried, most have wheels and a handle to make transport easier. However, at 100 pounds or more, picking them up to load or move may take two people. Appliances, power tools, or other devices can be plugged directly into standard outlets on the generator’s front panel.

Recent findings suggest that additionally, many models have a twist-lock plug that can provide up to 240 volts and be used to power circuits in a home via a manual transfer switch. You may hear generators like these referred to as “open frame” generators, which simply means that the engine, fuel tank, and generator components are not enclosed in bodywork.

Though inverter-type generators are—like their standard cousins—typically portable, we group them separately because they’re significantly and technically different in terms of how they work.

Like most generators, inverter generators provide 120/240 volts of AC power. They generate AC current just like the others, but it’s then converted to DC (Direct Current), and then inverted back to AC. The conversion and inversion is controlled by circuitry which acts like a filter, flattens surges, and cleans up the sine wave (or oscillating wave) of the electrical current.

In a recent development, typical generators have varying degrees of distortion in the sine wave of the alternating current. This isn’t usually an issue for most electrical devices, though sensitive electronics like tablets, laptops, televisions, and other smart devices can be damaged by current distortion or surges. These devices will last longer with “clean” power and steady voltage. Because of that added complication, inverter generators can be significantly more expensive.

Recent findings suggest that standby generators are permanently installed and connected to a home. These may power selected, critical circuits during a power outage, or may provide power for the whole home. Standby generators have systems that monitor power supplied by a utility and start automatically in the event of an outage. Since they’re not portable or easily moved, we didn’t include any here.

It’s vital to know what you intend to power with a generator in order to choose the right size. Manufacturers list two figures for generators: starting watts and running watts. Starting watts include the initial surge required to start appliances or tools with powerful electric motors or compressors. Once started, these devices require far less power to run continuously.

According to recent reports, many manufacturers have a chart with estimated power requirements for common appliances and tools to help you figure out what you need. For a more precise measurement, you can also calculate the figure yourself by adding up the power consumption of specific appliances and adding them together.

To calculate watts, multiply voltage (usually 120 volts) by the amps (amperage) required to run the appliance (usually found on a tag attached to the appliance). Do this for each item that the generator will power.

In a recent development, most portable generators are powered by gasoline, the most commonly available fuel. However, when using generators for emergency power, their infrequent use presents some concerns to consider.

It has been revealed that the first is that when big, catastrophic storms hit and power outages last for days, gas stations may struggle to meet demand, resulting in long lines. The second concern has to do with the infrequent use of backup generators, which may sit for months to years between uses.

Sources indicate that gasoline sitting in a carburetor will slowly evaporate over time, leaving gummy deposits that can block fuel from getting through, making it difficult or even impossible to start your generator without servicing. You can avoid this by closing the fuel valve and letting the generator run until it stalls, using up the remaining fuel in the carburetor. Also, over time, gasoline can oxidize or become “stale,” losing combustibility. It may also absorb water, which can then corrode fuel tanks and other metal components in the fuel system. Starting a generator regularly, as well as treating fuel with a stabilizer, can help fight these problems.

Ethanol-free gasoline, available at some gas stations, is also less susceptible to degradation over time than standard 87-octane pump gas; however, it’s still a good idea to mix the fuel going into your generator with stabilizer.

Recent findings suggest that dual-fuel generators can run on gasoline or liquified petroleum gas (LPG), commonly known as propane. Switching between the fuels is simple, and you won’t be tied to the availability of one type of fuel.

Industry observers note that A substantial advantage of propane is that it’s very stable when stored for long periods of time. It won’t go stale, and it won’t gum up carburetors from sitting. Plus, some homes that use propane for other purposes may already have large storage tanks on the premises, foregoing the need to make repeated trips out for fuel.

The downside to propane is that it creates fewer BTUs (British Thermal Units, a measurement of energy) than the same amount of gasoline. So, a generator running on propane will have slightly reduced starting and running watts. On the plus side, though, it will also run a little quieter than those that run on gasoline.

It has been revealed that while not as common, tri-fuel generators add an option to connect by natural gas. Some propane-powered generators can be converted to run on natural gas, as well. Like propane, natural gas can run cleaner and a little quieter. However, it also creates fewer BTUs than gasoline and propane, so it will also produce reduced starting and running watts.

Natural gas also requires a dedicated line for the generator, which most homes that have access to natural gas will not have, and thus will need to be professionally installed.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re powering appliances, tools, or other devices by plugging them directly into the standard outlets on the generator, the answer is no. If the generator is being used to power circuits in your home, maybe. It’s always best to consult the operator’s manual, a licensed electrician, or your local building officials about township ordinances—some localities may have requirements that differ from the National Electrical Code (NEC).

Electrical circuits need to be grounded to operate devices safely, so that any current that shorts out or has a fault is directed to the ground, i.e., the actual, literal earth, so the user doesn’t become the conduit to “ground.”.

There are two ways that generators are grounded: neutral-bonded and floating neutral. Neutral-bonded means the neutral wire is connected (i.e., bonded) to the generator frame. With a floating neutral, the neutral is not connected to the frame. In the latter case, the generator should be grounded by connecting the ground terminal to a grounding rod driven into the ground.

Industry observers note that generators with ground-fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) outlets, when used to power circuits in your home, require neutral switching and a manual transfer switch, and must be grounded by connecting the ground terminal to a ground rod driven into the soil. Neutral-switching transfer switches are also referred to as three-pole transfer switches.

In a recent development, there could be numerous reasons for difficulty starting a generator. The first things to check are whether or not there's any fuel in the tank, and if the fuel valve is turned open. Then, check for any obstructions in the air cleaner box. If that’s clean, move on to check that the engine has spark.

If your generator has sat for a long time without treated fuel, the carburetor may be clogged up and require cleaning—if you’re unfamiliar with any of these steps, it may be best to take it to a shop for service.

In an emergency, use what you can get, but as a general rule, 87 octane fuel will be fine—just don’t go lower than that.

Industry observers note that as long as we’re talking fuel, it’s always best to use ethanol-free fuel in equipment with small gas engines—if that’s not possible, nothing more than 10-percent ethanol. Ethanol can attract moisture, which will then separate and settle in the gas tank or carburetor, where it can corrode and clog the fuel system. For this reason, it’s also a good idea to treat gas with a fuel stabilizer.

Industry observers note that much like your lawn mower, generators need regular maintenance. However, since they often see less use, maintenance intervals tend to be farther apart. Typical maintenance would include changing oil, checking the air filter and changing it if needed, changing the fuel filter if so equipped, and checking the spark plug.

The best source of specific maintenance and troubleshooting information for your generator is the owner’s manual.

#135473. Astronomers catch ‘galaxy-killing’ wind in the act

Astronomers catch ‘galaxy-killing’ wind in the act

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1377 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the local universe, it is common to find galaxies that have stopped forming newly introduced stars.
  • According to recent reports, but ever since it first began surveying the cosmos, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has discovered more quiescent galaxies within the cosmos’ first 2 billion years than current models of galaxy formation and evolution predict.
  • Now, a team has found evidence that when galaxies collide — as they frequently did in the early universe — it can trigger a burst of star formation so intense that it generates winds capable of snuffing out the opportunity for any further stars to be born.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the local universe, it is common to find galaxies that have stopped forming newly introduced stars. These so-called quiescent galaxies have lived for billions of years and over that time, gradually exhausted their star-forming gas. By contrast, galaxies that lie at much greater distances — and thus appear to us when they were young, in the early universe — should have plenty of gas and be readily forming stars.

According to recent reports, but ever since it first began surveying the cosmos, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has discovered more quiescent galaxies within the cosmos’ first 2 billion years than current models of galaxy formation and evolution predict. Astronomers don’t know why they have stopped forming stars so soon, but they have many theories. Some of them require dark energy to have had a stronger influence in the early universe than previously thought, and thus have profound impacts on our understanding of the universe and its evolution.

Now, a team has found evidence that when galaxies collide — as they frequently did in the early universe — it can trigger a burst of star formation so intense that it generates winds capable of snuffing out the opportunity for any further stars to be born. This could explain the high number of young but unexpectedly quiescent galaxies JWST has found without needing drastic changes to our understanding of dark energy and its influence over time.

In order to form stars, galaxies need reservoirs of gas that are dense and cold, lacking energy and prone to collapsing inward. One way to end a galaxy’s era of star formation — a process that astronomers call quenching — is to trigger strong winds that blast outward from the galaxy. These vast, high-speed flows of charged particles can blow away or heat this cold gas.

Industry observers note that such galactic winds can have two possible sources of energy. One is an actively accreting central supermassive black hole (called an active galactic nucleus, or AGN). The other is the energetic blasts generated by massive stars that form and then quickly die, ending their lives by exploding as supernovae. But astronomers have never caught such a wind in the act of draining its host of gas in the early universe, as it is difficult to get a detailed look inside a galaxy so far away.

To better discern the inner workings of star-forming galaxies in the early universe, researchers carried out a joint survey combining observations taken with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) — a powerful radio observatory in Chile — and infrared data from JWST. They also turned to archival data from the Hubble Space Telescope. A team led by astrophysicist Rebecca Davies of Swinburne University of Technology in Australia spotted one particular galaxy, called CRISTAL-02, that highlights what appears to be the first direct evidence of a wind powerful enough to halt star formation in a massive galaxy just 1.1 billion years after the Big Bang. The discovery was published June 10 in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.

CRISTAL-02 is part of a larger sample of around two dozen star-forming galaxies at a similar distance (and therefore of a similar age). Observations revealed a huge plume of cold gas extending outside the galaxy, almost as large as the galaxy it comes from. The plume is moving toward Earth at some 60 miles (100 kilometers) per second. Finding fast-moving gas so far from the galaxy is a sign the gas is being actively pushed out in a wind-driven process.

Sources indicate that but to truly determine the nature of the plume, the team first had to rule out another possibility behind its formation: Because CRISTAL-02 also appears to be in the throes of merging with several other galaxies, the plume could be a tidal tail — gas stripped away by gravitational forces during the interaction, rather than a genuine wind. This was tricky to determine, Davies indicates, as no single measurement could settle the question of the gas’ origin; instead the team had to combine several different measurements to characterize the plume and confirm its cause.

First, Davies’ team measured how many upcoming stars the galaxy produces each year. Massive stars live much shorter lives than less massive ones, so looking at how many young, massive stars are in a galaxy indicates how rapidly it is forming new stars to replace the ones that are dying. So, the team searched for signs of these young, massive stars in the galaxy’s spectrum and measured how bright those features appear.

It has been revealed that the researchers also needed to determine how much gas the galaxy is losing. They did so by first using ALMA data to calculate the mass in the plume and then combining it with the gas’ velocity and distance from the galaxy’s center.

It has been revealed that the verdict: CRISTAL-02 is forming stars at roughly three times the rate of a typical galaxy its size at this distance, but is losing twice as much gas as the galaxy’s star-formation rate. “If this rapid blowout continues, the galaxy could be dead in less than 50 million years, explaining the origin of the mysterious massive dead galaxies in the early universe,” Davies mentioned in a press release.

Finally, the team turned to identifying the cause of the plume. Was the gas being pushed out by energy coming from the galaxy’s central black hole, or was the galaxy’s burst of intense star formation — and the resulting supernova blasts — the culprit?

Sources indicate that models predict that the most powerful outflows from massive galaxies like these should be the result of accretion onto supermassive black holes, Davies states. But CRISTAL-02 highlights no sign of AGN activity in its center. On the other hand, based on the amount of massive young stars in the galaxy, Davies’ team calculated that the energy transferred to the surrounding gas as these stars die and explode as supernovae would be powerful enough to produce the observed plume.

The speed of the gas backs this idea up. Supernova-driven outflows rarely exceed speeds of about 1,550 miles (2,500 km) per second, indicates Christy Tremonti, an astronomer at the University of Wisconsin–Madison who was not involved in the study. Velocities higher than this usually point to an AGN as the energy source. CRISTAL-02’s outflow is moving around 400 miles (640 km) per second, comfortably within the range expected for a wind produced by a powerful starburst.

Davies notes that “the result is surprising,” going against the conventional wisdom that AGN are the cause of star-formation-ending winds. Tremonti notes that  “theoretical models love to use AGN feedback to shut off star formation in massive galaxies — almost every simulation does.” Yet CRISTAL-02’s star formation alone appears capable of triggering a wind that could exhaust its gas supply within tens of millions of years.

Recent findings suggest that CRISTAL-02’s story may not be an isolated case, Davies states. Studies suggest that around 40% of massive star-forming galaxies in the early universe are merging, meaning many of them may be caught in similar growth spurts. If this commonly results in subsequent supernova-driven winds, it could help explain why so many early galaxies burned brightly and died young. “It may be the case that AGN are really notable for keeping star formation off, but maybe they’re not the thing that shuts it down initially,” Tremonti says.

The case isn’t entirely closed. Davies states her team cannot completely rule out the presence of an active supermassive black hole — either one too faint to detect, or one that may have flared briefly in the past and pushed gas away from the galaxy before subsequently fading from view. Tremonti agrees this is one of the hardest scenarios to eliminate. Future observations in the mid-infrared, which can peer through dust that might otherwise hide a buried black hole, could help close this gap.

As for CRISTAL-02, its fate is somewhat ironic: The explosive burst of star formation it is undergoing is also the underlying cause of its imminent death.

According to recent reports, shreejaya Karantha is a science writer based in India. Her work has appeared in Sky & Telescope, Phys.org, Live Science US, and The Hindu.

Phaethon’s fiery folly

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (407 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Astronomy

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, even the best-laid aims can require a bit of luck to execute.
  • In a recent development, “I deliberately positioned myself near a local airport in the hope that an aircraft might cross the Sun during the eclipse,” he tells Astronomy.
  • Industry observers note that the work wasn’t over: The image “required a somewhat more elaborate workflow” than the conventional stacking and sharpening of video frames.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, even the best-laid aims can require a bit of luck to execute. During the solar eclipse of Aug. 12, 2026, in which parts of Iceland, Portugal, and Spain experienced totality, much of western Europe enjoyed a substantial partial eclipse. Astrophotographer Alexandre Tournay set up near Brussels to capture the Moon crossing the disk — as well as a transit of another kind.

In a recent development, “I deliberately positioned myself near a local airport in the hope that an aircraft might cross the Sun during the eclipse,” he tells Astronomy. “Against the odds, one did, passing across the partially eclipsed solar disk with its contrail trailing behind it.” Flight tracking data allowed him to pinpoint the flight: Cargolux 5933, a Boeing 747 freighter from Mexico City bound for Luxembourg.

Industry observers note that the work wasn’t over: The image “required a somewhat more elaborate workflow” than the conventional stacking and sharpening of video frames. That process brings out the roiling details in the Sun’s chromosphere, but would oversharpen the edges of the airplane and Moon. So Tournay blended a 1,000-frame stack of the Sun with a single frame that preserved the silhouettes and froze their motion against the disk.

Sources indicate that he named the resulting image “Phaethon’s Flight” after the boy in Greek mythology who journeyed east to prove that his father was Helios, the Sun god. Phaethon convinced Helios to let him drive his Sun-bearing chariot across the sky, but was unable to control the horses. He blazed an erratic path that brought climatic extremes to Earth — freezing cold and scorching heat — before Zeus intervened and struck him down dead.

According to recent reports, “There’s something fascinating about being able to photograph, with modern instruments, a celestial phenomenon that our ancestors could only understand and describe through mythology,” claims Tournay. “And then, by pure chance, to have a flying machine cross the Sun at that exact moment, almost as though a modern-day chariot were dragging the eclipse behind it across the sky, made the story of Phaethon feel like a perfect fit. Seeing that plane cross the eclipsed Sun, I can almost hear the ancients screaming, ‘See?! I told you it was Phaethon!’ ”.

Mark Zastrow is Editor-in-Chief of Astronomy magazine. He holds masters degrees in astronomy and science journalism and has over a decade of experience covering science in the U.S. and in Asia.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Recent findings suggest that in 1973, U.S. Senator Ted Kennedy often visited the cancer ward at Boston Children’s Hospital, where his eldest son was battling osteosarcoma. Kennedy witnessed other parents on the ward make impossible decisions regarding their child’s care when insurance didn’t cover it. Their stories lit a fire within the senator that burned bright for the rest of his life.

Kennedy spent decades fighting for health care reform, representing his home state of Massachusetts. He even teamed up with a former political rival from across the aisle: Mitt Romney. The story of this unexpected alliance is recounted in Mitt & Ted, the newest season of the GBH News podcast The Substantial Dig. Over eight episodes, journalist and host Ian Coss explores how their work laid the foundation for the Affordable Care Act, one of the most significant and divisive health care reforms in U.S. history.

Sources indicate that we first meet Romney as a young upstart Republican challenger vying to flip Kennedy’s Senate seat in 1994. The race seemed close until a legendary debate. Romney had Kennedy on the defensive until the sitting senator pivoted to the matter near and dear to his heart: health care.

Sources indicate that “Kennedy is the elder statesman, in command of the matter,” Coss says. “Romney is like an eager student trying to pass the test.” Using his deep knowledge, Kennedy buries the less experienced Romney. In the election, Kennedy then beat Romney by a landslide, even when many Democrats were ousted by Republican challengers that same year. But the loss may have motivated Romney to keep going.

In a recent development, several years later, Romney unexpectedly became a champion of health care reform as the newly elected governor of Massachusetts. The state’s health care system was facing the potential loss of about a billion dollars in federal funding, threatening hospitals that served vulnerable populations. Romney’s administration created Romneycare, which was supported by three features: individual and employer mandates, affordable options for low-income people, and a health care exchange where people could compare plans from different providers.

With Senator Kennedy’s help, the groundbreaking law passed in 2006 and expanded health insurance coverage to 98 percent of Massachusetts’ population.

Romneycare gained national attention and kicked off years-long efforts to replicate it on the federal level. Finally, in 2010, President Obama signed the Affordable Care Act, or ACA. Modeled on Romneycare, the law (colloquially called Obamacare) adapted the reforms made in Massachusetts for all 50 states, a challenge since many states had larger shares of uninsured people than Massachusetts had even before Romneycare.

The Democrats in Congress also sought to include a government insurance proposal in the reform, similar to Medicaid but available to more people. Republicans were wary of the ACA generally, but a government-provided insurance option was a line they wouldn’t cross. The ACA eventually passed without the public option, but by then the political winds had shifted. If there ever was a chance to secure bipartisan support for the law, it was gone by the time Democrats were willing to compromise on the public option. And as soon as the ACA became law, Republicans started fighting it.

Industry observers note that the podcast traces an impressive number of political twists and turns on this health care reform journey. Though I got turned around a few times, I never fully lost the plot thanks to Coss’ well-placed reminders and takeaways.

Beyond the story of Romney and Kennedy, the podcast gives voice to many more people who made the ACA a reality: government workers who went from foes to allies who enlisted unlikely help from the conservative Heritage Foundation; longtime friends in the Massachusetts state legislature who were driven apart by the reform; a father who struggled to afford health care and how he advocated for reform with his church. I teared up more than once listening to the human stories behind these policy changes.

In a recent development, overall, Mitt & Ted gave me new appreciation for why passing a reform is so difficult, despite how life-changing and life-saving access to health care can be. The series points to moments when stars aligned to make reform possible and suggests that more of those opportunities lie ahead.

Industry observers note that “The work of American health care remains very much unfinished,” Coss indicates. “When the perfect alignment of frustration and opportunity arrives again, that might be what determines whether our leaders actually work together.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
