#135376. Tech Report: The 8 Best Trail Cameras for Hunting, Wildlife Watching, and Even Home Security

📅 21 Sep 2021 • ⏱️ 25m • 📚 Deep Dive (5051 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popularmechanics ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: The 8 Best Trail Cameras for Hunting, Wildlife Watching, and Even Home Security

📅 21 Sep 2021 | ⏱️ 25 min read (5051 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~25 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Fall is peak season for those who want to gather last-minute information on deer and other game animals ahead of hunting seasons.
  • The advantage of having a modern trail camera is the ability to capture the action you’d otherwise miss, whether it’s an elusive buck passing by your stand in the night or the raccoon creating backyard mayhem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Fall is peak season for those who want to gather last-minute information on deer and other game animals ahead of hunting seasons. Even if you’re not heading into the woods to hunt, it’s one of the most interesting times of year for observing wild animals. Whitetail deer, elk, bears, and other animals are becoming much more active due to seasonal mating periods while waterfowl and other birds migrate for the winter.

The advantage of having a modern trail camera is the ability to capture the action you’d otherwise miss, whether it’s an elusive buck passing by your stand in the night or the raccoon creating backyard mayhem. If you’re considering a trail camera that uses a cellular network to send photos and videos directly to your smartphone, the good news is these have gotten even easier to use.

Industry observers note that while the trail cam experience improves every year, the cost of many units is more than $100, and cellular models require recurring data plan charges, making it trickier to assess value. Images from game cameras are better than ever, even in budget models, and apps add software features often.

Sorting out what matters most to you and how you blueprint to use your trail cameras can be a challenge, so we explain what to look for along with sharing our top recommendations selected from year-round testing of dozens of cameras evaluated side-by-side.

The Tactacam Reveal Pro 4.0 replaces the Reveal Pro 3.0 camera, our previous pick for Best Overall. Released this summer, the Pro 4.0 version keeps what made the 3.0 great and improves on it in two key areas: image quality and battery life. Reveal has one of the best apps in the space, with tons of settings and features to tweak your setup and manage your cameras and images. Updates to these basics are massive usability improvements that demanding trail camera users will notice.

Cameras going dead in the field is a major gripe for people of these gadgets. You have to physically go and replace batteries, which adds hassle and cost to your experience. I tend to place cameras in early summer and let them run for several months until my hunting season starts. The problem is that active cameras can run through eight to 12 AA batteries in a month depending on the model and your camera settings.

It has been revealed that tactacam has tackled this issue in a few ways with the Pro 4.0 release. The brand told me it audited everything about camera operation that drained the battery and then made small tweaks to reduce power demands anywhere it could.

Tactacam has also developed sold separately R5 and R10 lithium battery packs that replace previous battery add-ons, which have the notable benefit of swapping into the same form factor as the AA battery tray, so they don’t add bulk to the camera.

Image quality in the Reveal cameras has always been solid, but the tech giant took a unique approach to dealing with the challenge of getting both crisp day and night images by installing separate sensors for each. Photographers know that night images require different gear and settings than daylight shooting, so the split makes sense. The early returns from a month of testing confirm that the quality of both day and night is much improved.

Industry observers note that the rest of this flagship Reveal camera is impressive, carrying over from the Pro 3.0 and now-discontinued Ultra camera. The Reveal lineup now has just two similar cameras: the Pro 4.0 and the X 4.0. The Reveal X 4.0 is basically the Pro 4.0 without a built-in display screen, which saves $30 and is a great option if you don’t value the screen for aiming and reviewing images at the device.

According to recent reports, as mentioned, the robust app gives you remote control over everything including photo and video capture settings, transmission frequency, night image flash, trigger delays, and more. You’re also able to launch a live stream to follow up on interesting images, but there’s an additional subscription cost and it will drain the battery promptly. There’s also built-in GPS that demonstrates the location of your camera on a map within the app—essential if you’ve forgotten where you placed it or if it’s stolen.

Full Tactacam Reveal Pro 4.0 Review.

Cell-connected trail cameras are handy, but if you’re low on funds or trying to run a multitude of cameras, paying $150 and up per camera gets pricey fast. Spypoint’s Flex M2 trail camera keeps both the upfront purchase cost and recurring subscription fees reasonable. Spypoint even has a free data plan that gives you 100 images per month if you want to avoid subscription fees altogether. (The Flex M2 doesn’t have onboard memory, nor does it ship with an SD card, so you’ll have to spend at least another $20 per camera for a high-speed SD card.).

Despite the low price, the camera’s 32-megapixel photos and 1080p video are clear and well-exposed. The Flex M2 displays lower-resolution images in the app but you can request full-resolution images when you want more detail. This is beneficial because it keeps data demands low and indicates up in the battery usage as well. After a month in the field, the eight AA batteries I was using displayed in the app at “High” strength.

Additionally, I appreciated that this camera is compact since I’m usually hauling my cameras several miles into the backcountry in a pack. If you want to run this camera year-round, I’d consider picking up the $60 five-watt solar panel add-on, which has a built-in battery and should allow you to leave the Flex M2 up indefinitely.

According to recent reports, I was impressed with the overall experience with the Flex M2, but the highlight here is the cost to purchase and run this camera. Yes, you’ll need to pay up for video or a higher quota of images, but this is a great option if you want the excitement of getting trail camera images on your phone without the annoyance of yet another recurring subscription fee on your credit card.

According to recent reports, there are two significant recurring costs with a cellular trail camera: the data strategy and batteries. Connected cameras can chew through batteries, which can add up, especially since you’ll want to use more expensive lithium batteries if you can. Sehmua’s 4G Solar Trail Camera comes with rechargeable batteries and a solar panel, which allows the camera to run indefinitely given adequate sun exposure.

The camera itself has a fast trigger and 2K photo and video that can be saved to an SD card, or to cloud storage for an additional cost. The app, which is a little clunky and can be confusing due to some quirky menus and word choices, works with images that show up swiftly and reliably.

Notably, even though this is a 4G cellular-connected camera, you can still use the camera to record to the SD card if you decide not to pay for one of the data looks. This is another sneaky way this camera provides solid value for its low price point.

Full Sehmua Trail Camera Review.

The best way to cut down on battery costs for your trail cameras is running solar panels. While many cameras have the option to run on solar, it’s often an additional upfront cost. The newly introduced 2026 Moultrie Edge 4 Solar trail camera has it all smartly packaged together in an integrated unit that costs less than some standalone cameras.

Industry observers note that setting up solar often requires separate mounting as well as hauling out lots of separate pieces and cables to be connected. The Edge 4 Solar just straps to a tree as a single unit, ready to run indefinitely. The camera comes with a rechargeable lithium-ion battery powered by the panel, which enables you to place a camera and leave it running as long as you need. Having the solar panel integrated is convenient and compact, but you’ll need to choose spots wisely to ensure both good captures and sun exposure.

Sources indicate that beyond the solar power setup, the Edge 4 is a solid trail camera with crisp 40-megapixel photos and 1080p video. The app is polished and makes setup and use hassle-free even if you’re not particularly tech-savvy. The subscription prepares are in line with the industry average, ranging from $8.99 to $22.99. The lowest-tier strategy offers more than most other companies’ $5 plans (1,000 images and 10 videos) and the most expensive plan offers unlimited images and 50 videos and discounts steeply to $7.99 per month for each additional camera.

It has been revealed that the convenience of cell-connected trail cameras is undeniable, but if you’re burned out on subscription charges and don’t mind checking your cameras manually, you can save a significant amount on your trail camera setup. The WOSPORTS Trail Camera is a budget option with impressive image quality and low one-time cost. The camera doesn’t ship with the required eight AA batteries, but it does come with an SD card.

This compact G600 records imagery to an SD card and lasts longer since it doesn’t use batteries communicating over cellular networks. You’ll have to walk into your hunting zone to swap cards, but the purchase price is a fraction of the lifetime cost of buying and operating a modern cell-connected setup.

According to recent reports, the 56-megapixel images and 4K video aren’t Planet Earth–level quality, but I was still more than satisfied with the pictures and videos I got. I don’t put too much stock in megapixel numbers as a true measure of trail camera image quality because these numbers are mostly inflated with software enhancements. That noted, the images and videos from the WOSPORTS camera were sharp enough for clear identification of details.

The Defend by Reveal 360 is not your traditional trail camera—it’s closer to a home security camera that’s designed to work anywhere. Ring and other doorbell cameras usually rely on WiFi for connectivity, which makes them impractical more than about 50 yards from your router. The Defend 360 uses cellular networks instead so you can place this camera anywhere with a decent cell signal.

According to recent reports, in the field, the Defend 360’s biggest advantage is motion. Most trail cams are fixed in place, but this one adds remote pan-and-tilt control, allowing you to reposition the camera from your phone. Its 355-degree pan and 75-degree tilt effectively eliminate blind spots when combined with the wide-angle lens.

Industry observers note that like a regular trail camera, motion detection triggers photos only to conserve battery and data. A 1080p live view can be activated on demand when you need a closer live look. That approach makes sense for remote monitoring, though it feels different if you’re used to continuous video feeds from home security cameras.

It has been revealed that A rechargeable battery and included solar panel allow for long-term deployment with minimal maintenance. Setup is straightforward via the app, and the camera automatically connects to the strongest available carrier via eSIM.

Recent findings suggest that there are a few downsides. Night footage is serviceable but not amazing, and like most cellular cameras, it requires a subscription plan to unlock full functionality. Still, if your goal is reliable, wide-area monitoring in remote locations, the Defend 360 delivers better coverage and control than standard trail cameras.

A lifetime warranty usually isn’t reason enough alone to buy a product, but in the world of electronics generally and with trail cameras specifically, it’s unheard of and fairly compelling.

It has been revealed that with Yellowstone.ai’s Y2 Camera and Solar Bundle, your upfront cost is on the higher side at $250, but the solar panel and rechargeable battery mean no recurring battery costs. You’ll also save on gas and time, since this is a cell-connected camera, and there’s no need to visit the camera unless you want to move it.

Compared to the substantial-name trail camera apps, the app is not quite as polished, but over several months of testing, I did not experience any of the quirks and bugs I’ve experienced with some trail cam apps from overseas companies (Yellowstone.ai is U.S.-based).

It has been revealed that the image and video quality isn’t quite as sharp as the top tier of the cameras I’ve tested like the Reveal Pro 4.0 or Moultrie Edge 4 Solar, but it’s by no means unacceptable. I was impressed by features such as built-in GPS, automatic cell network selection, and remote settings adjustments.

The solar bundle comes with the panel, Y2 camera, and two rechargeable battery packs. If you want to keep the upfront cost down, the camera alone is half the price at $125.

Sources indicate that no matter how great your trail camera placement, it’s easy for cameras to miss animals. This is exacerbated in big open areas such as wetlands or crop fields where it can be hard to know precisely where animals might appear.

Muddy’s Trifecta 180 is built to minimize these misses. Three motion sensors and a rotating camera capture wide-angle 180-degree images. This is the perfect camera for the edge of large agricultural fields where animals could appear anywhere and often turn up in groups that can be hard to capture in a single image. You have the option for the camera to stitch together impressive panorama images (though they’re harder to appreciate on a phone screen) or the option to capture single-zone images like a regular trail camera would.

Sources indicate that the downside of this impressive device is that it seemed to use more battery power than usual, likely attributable to the camera’s need to move and the usual drains of taking and transmitting images. If you’re planning on running it long-term, I’d consider picking up the solar panel accessory with integrated battery.

Sources indicate that I’ve assembled my choices in this guide based on years of firsthand testing, and I continue testing latest trail cam options every season to keep up with the constant rollout of new features and improvements. For decades, I’ve been hanging trail cameras with professional hunters and friends to capture wallowing elk, nursing moose, and scavenging bears on camera.

Industry observers note that historically, I’ve preferred inexpensive, simple cameras that I monitor manually, which keeps my trail camera budget in check, but as connected cameras have gotten more reliable and affordable, I’ve shifted to using cell cams almost exclusively. I hunt in three different states as well as in spots several hours from my home in Colorado, which makes manually checking all my cameras nearly impossible. I still employ “manual” cameras around my property where pulling memory cards frequently isn’t a pain.

It has been revealed that one of the main divisions in the trail camera market is whether your trail camera connects to a cellular network, which, if it does, is what allows you to wirelessly send images over great distances. Connected models are so common now that AT&T and Verizon offer monthly service prepares that often come bundled with the camera.

Sources indicate that this connectivity means that you don’t have to physically visit your camera to check out the imagery it has captured—a benefit that’s most tangible when cameras are placed in far-flung hunting spots, but less valuable if you’re using the camera closer to your house. The cellular connection also makes the cameras easier to operate since most cell-connected cameras can be controlled via your smartphone through apps. These allow you to use remote-control camera settings to switch between photo and video modes, adjust camera sensitivity, and check battery levels.

Networked cameras are addictive to use because they can provide instant, or at least frequent, gratification from your camera(s). However, there’s usually a recurring data proposal cost in addition to setup complexity. Bottom line: Be sure you really need the connectivity. There also may be legal restrictions on wirelessly connected cameras that limit how you can use them. Be sure to double-check your state’s regulations before buying.

In a recent development, all trail cameras store images locally on the device, whether or not they have the ability to transmit them wirelessly. More often than not, that storage comes in the form of an SD or micro SD card, which you can remove to download your photos. Cameras with wireless support, however, now often feature an internal hard drive, which stores data more reliably, since you no longer need to physically “pull cards” to collect your footage.

If you’re planning to only use a networked camera, I recommend choosing a camera with internal memory. The No. 1 source of problems I’ve had over the years of testing dozens of different trail cameras and helping others set up many more is memory cards. These plastic chip-like cards are fragile, easy to lose, and can be formatted incorrectly. Even when there’s nothing wrong with a card, cheaper SD cards with slower transfer speeds can cause errors when processing larger images and videos.

In a recent development, the only advantage of having a camera with removable memory is if you want to use the camera without a data blueprint. This is required for the increasingly rare non-networked cameras, but even connected cameras can be used manually if they have physical cards. Some cameras with internal memory also have an optional SD card slot, such as the Reveal Pro 3.0, which gives you the option to expand storage capacity and use the camera without paying for a data plan.

Sources indicate that this might seem like a minor detail, but given that many people want their trail camera to capture their subjects without alerting those subjects to the camera’s presence, the camera’s exterior color can be a critical factor. Since a majority of trail cameras are marketed to hunters and are intended to be used outdoors, these devices generally come in solid earth tones or camouflage patterns.

In a recent development, if you’re a hunter, you probably already have a good sense of what patterns are most appropriate for your area. If not, snap some photos of the trunks of the trees where you intend to mount the camera; then compare them to the patterns on the cameras you’re considering.

In a recent development, cameron Shrum, avid bowhunter and co-owner of C&K Archery in Frisco, Colorado, notes, “People will get a good deal on a camera and not realize how important it is to have [it] match [their] habitat. The goal is to get pictures of animals without them knowing they are being watched, and when something is out of place, game animals have a tendency to figure it out.”.

It has been revealed that as a professional photographer and videographer, the first thing you need to know about judging the quality of a camera is that there is no single metric that easily tells you which camera will record more clearly. At a glance, checking specs like the number of megapixels in a camera’s sensor gives you a decent clue as to what you can expect.

Industry observers note that ultimately, the best way to gauge the quality of a trail camera is with your eyes. Take a minute to look at sample photos posted by customers on retailers such as Amazon, which give you a practical way to evaluate images taken under natural conditions.

Recent findings suggest that trail cameras rarely take print-worthy shots, but that isn’t what they’re for. If you’re just patterning animals, image quality isn’t as crucial as simply detecting them. Trophy hunters trying to identify certain calibers of animals or monitor a specific animal across multiple cameras will want to be more picky about image quality and clarity.

Sources indicate that even if you don’t need great fidelity, a better image makes using trail cams more useful and rewarding. I’ve come to appreciate having modern trail cameras that deliver clear images and 4K videos over the crude, fuzzy work of older, lo-fi models.

It has been revealed that I recommend using only lithium batteries in trail cameras. Especially with cheaper cameras, I’ve found that regular alkaline batteries don’t provide enough voltage for the IR flash, and many times a trail camera may not record video with underpowered batteries (alkaline batteries start decreasing in voltage as soon as you start using them). Lithium batteries deliver higher voltage consistently, and they work better in the cold.

Sources indicate that if you’re setting up a cellular trail cam, make sure you check signal strength in the area. If you have a camera that offers an app or website (as many now do) that lets you view images on your smartphone, try triggering the camera and see if you receive the notification and image.

Since trail cameras are often left alone for days, weeks, or even months at a time, setting them up properly is important. Shrum recommends testing your trail camera before you walk away. “Have it snap a few pictures with you walking by and then review them. Sometimes you may not have the right angle; it may be too high or too low. Try to set the height and angle to capture the game in the center of the camera’s view.”.

In a recent development, trail cameras are usually strapped to a tree and most come packaged with a long strap for this purpose. If you’re placing a camera somewhere without convenient trees for the angle you want, look into a camera stand or even a tripod. Most trail cameras have a standard tripod plate mount (¼-20) and stands or stakes are available from most manufacturers.

According to recent reports, A common spot to place cameras is along well-traveled game trails. A tip I picked up watching champion archer Levi Morgan put up cameras on one of his hunting leases: rather than pointing the camera down a trail where it’s likely to be in the line-of-sight of animals as they walk it, put the camera off-trail between 10 and 30 feet away perpendicular to the trail. This will usually give you broadside images of animals instead of head-on and puts the camera in their periphery.

Once you’ve tested your placement (and image transmission for connected cameras) by viewing a test photo on the app or the camera itself, scan the camera’s field of view for latest-growth vegetation. Plants and tree branches can result in a near-constant stream of false triggers on a windy day. I like to place any plants or branches I cut behind the camera for a bit of concealment, making sure they can’t blow in front of the camera.

Since trail cams are motion-activated, a fast trigger seems important. You don’t want an animal to pass by the camera before you get a photo, right? In my experience, the real problem is taking the photo too quickly, which results in seeing just the nose of a slow-moving deer. Still, many brands tout their fast trigger speeds as if they solve an important problem.

In a recent development, “It’s kind of a BS spec, frankly,” Gregg Farrell, vice president of marketing for Tactacam Reveal, told me. “The goal is to capture the animal in the center of the frame and our cameras do that through the operating system working with the [motion] sensor.”.

Sources indicate that most trail cameras have listed trigger speeds around a half second, which can work well, but are often too quick if implemented poorly. I almost always switch my cameras to shoot a multishot burst, if available, to give the camera more opportunities to grab a well-framed shot. Keep in mind, though, that this will double or triple the number of images you receive, so it may not be a solution if you’re using a cell-connected camera and trying to save with a limited-data blueprint.

According to recent reports, some cameras have detection delay settings that let you set a period of time after an image is captured before it’ll take another. This can cut down on look-alike images if an animal is hanging around in the detection area, especially if you’ve enabled a multishot mode.

According to recent reports, connected trail cameras make scouting convenient, but they come with hidden costs. Almost all cellular trail cameras require a monthly data blueprint to cover the cost of cloud storage and image transmission.

In a recent development, many companies tack on extra fees for features such as live streaming, which eat up a lot of data and cost the companies money with their network provider partners. Like sitting at a blackjack table, it’s easy to get caught up in the excitement of scouting and click your way to hundreds of dollars in recurring monthly charges. You can review the details of each manufacturer’s data plans before you buy and decide what features you want to use in advance. You can save money on a camera if you decide you don’t need all the latest features and avoid the temptation of activating those extra charges in the process.

In a recent development, common game animals such as whitetail deer and elk tend to settle into routines during the summer months which often persist into early fall. The change of seasons and seasonal mating windows will help throw routine out the window in the fall, but if you can identify high-traffic areas in the spring and early summer, that will likely continue all summer.

The best practices for finding a good spot and setting up the camera properly are the same in any season. Spring in some ways makes it easier to identify animal travel patterns since the ground is often wet and recent activity is more obvious. Hike your zone and look for fresh signs to identify intersections, pinch points, and frequently visited locations. If you’re able to access your cameras easily and often, use the early season to experiment with different locations for a few weeks and try new spots you hadn’t considered before that show promise based on animal signs. Half the fun of placing these cameras is finding that perfect location and image framing that yields a ton of exciting wildlife images.

Recent findings suggest that there are plenty of things that can trigger a trail camera other than the type(s) of animals you’re looking to capture, including squirrels, lights, and vegetation moving in the wind. “False triggers,” as we call them, are not only disappointing, but waste storage and burn through your data initiative. It’s hard to eliminate them completely, but there are lots of ways to minimize them.

The most important is proper camera setup. Once you’ve got it framed up the way you want and have a successful test image, look for branches and weeds in the frame, primarily in the foreground. A single goldenrod stalk or pine bough can burn through a month’s data allotment on a windy day, so take your time to clear the immediate area in front of your camera.

Recent findings suggest that you can’t always clear cut in front of a camera, so if you find you’re still getting more false triggers than you’d like, adjust the camera’s trigger sensitivity down. Many cameras only offer high or low, but if you have a more finely graded adjustment such as the 1 through 10 sensitivity settings on the Reveal Pro 3.0, adjust slowly down until you stop getting false triggers so you don’t overcorrect and miss animals.

Sources indicate that some cameras also use recognition software to reject images that appear to be empty. Moultrie’s Edge cameras allow you to only accept motion triggers in selected zones of an image, effectively blocking triggers from, for example, a corner of a detection zone with moving tree branches.

Most states have some sort of regulation with the use of trail cameras, especially when used on public land and as they relate to hunting activities. Arizona, where game animals tend to congregate around limited water sources, banned trail cameras for hunting statewide in 2021. Colorado, where I live, has few restrictions on trail camera use before your hunting season begins, but limits employing them while you’re actively hunting.

Using trail cameras on your own private property doesn’t usually involve too many restrictions, but be sure to check the regulations from your state’s wildlife management organization to confirm, as private land practices can still be regulated through the hunting codes since wildlife are considered a shared public resource.

There are so many options for security cameras dedicated to home use, and because of that, most of the time it makes more sense to just buy a security camera from a brand that specializes in that application, such as Ring or Google Nest.

These products generally have superior apps and software to hunt-focused trail cameras. Since they're designed for home use, they effortlessly connect to your home WiFi network, don’t require a data subscription, and will have features trail cameras won’t such as two-way communication.

In a recent development, that said, if you already own trail cameras and don’t need specific features, most trail cameras can serve a security purpose. The best trail cameras to employ for security are the newer “live” trail cameras that transmit imagery instantly via cell networks and notify you on your phone when the camera has been triggered.

Another option is WiFi-enabled trail cameras that can connect to your phone without a cellular network to transmit images. However, these cameras don’t usually transmit if you’re not within range of the camera (i.e., at home), so they’re limited to general monitoring rather than real-time notification when you’re away.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

A bill introduced by Sen. Katie Britt on Wednesday aims to combat a rising diversity of financial fraud by unifying the U.S. effort to fight it.

It has been revealed that the draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts. It is aimed at ensuring that federal agencies, law enforcement, financial institutions, telecommunications and technology companies and other groups work together, according to an overview from Britt.

The fresh office would promote intelligence sharing across the public and private sectors, coordinate consumer education efforts and improve assistance for victims.

Britt, R-Ala., said the effort is needed because fraudsters operate nimbly utilizing social media while taking advantage of fragmented or disorganized responses from individual companies and government agencies.

Sources indicate that “This effort is about bringing everyone to the table and making sure our response keeps pace with the criminals who are exploiting newly introduced technologies and gaps between sectors,” she noted in a statement. “When we work together to identify threats earlier and share information more effectively, we can better protect American families and businesses.”.

The office would develop a “lexicon of fraud” so that terms for different kinds of scams are standardized between various federal law enforcement agencies to promote a “whole-of-government response,” a Britt aide said.

The office also would work to broaden the approach to combating fraud beyond just having financial institutions reimburse victims. It would tap telecommunications and technology companies to address fraud at its source, such as rip-offs that start as text messages, social media posts or online advertisements.

Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. She is the sponsor of a bill that would allow state, local and tribal law enforcement agencies to use federal grant funding to investigate financial fraud, particularly scams targeted at the elderly.

The measure highlights the prevalence of "pig butchering," a common technique where a predator cultivates a personal relationship with a victim over many months to extract the most cash.

In a recent development, the House passed its version of the bill in September with overwhelming bipartisan support. The House sponsor is Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa.

Recent findings suggest that senior financial abuse also was the focus of a bill the House passed in an overwhelming 414-2 vote in June. The legislation, sponsored by Rep. Ann Wagner, R-Mo., would codify Securities and Exchange Commission guidance that permits mutual funds and their agents to postpone the sale of securities if there is a reasonable belief that financial exploitation of someone who is elderly or disabled is occurring.

It's not clear whether the Senate will take action on these bills or Britt's by the end of the year.

“If it doesn’t get through in the lame duck, it will continue to be a priority in the 120th [Congress],” the Britt aide said.

Cristian Mungiu’s Latest Drama Fjord Plunges Into the Depths of Coastal Norway

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1296 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television indicates, and more.
  • Following in the footsteps of Anatomy of a Fall and Sentimental Value, Cristian Mungiu’s fresh film Fjord continues a recent trend of complex, critically acclaimed family dramas set against a gorgeous—if appropriately chilly—European backdrop.
  • In a recent development, loosely based on a real court case, Fjord follows a devout evangelical Romanian man named Mihai (Sebastian Stan) and his Norwegian wife Lisbet (Renate Reinsve) who move to a remote fjord village in Norway with their five children.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television indicates, and more. This time, we take a look at Fjord.

Following in the footsteps of Anatomy of a Fall and Sentimental Value, Cristian Mungiu’s fresh film Fjord continues a recent trend of complex, critically acclaimed family dramas set against a gorgeous—if appropriately chilly—European backdrop. The Romanian New Wave director won his second Palme d’Or at this year’s Cannes Film Festival for the Norway-set film, which is also his first shot outside of his home country and Romania’s official selection for the best international feature category at the 2027 Oscars.

In a recent development, loosely based on a real court case, Fjord follows a devout evangelical Romanian man named Mihai (Sebastian Stan) and his Norwegian wife Lisbet (Renate Reinsve) who move to a remote fjord village in Norway with their five children. Their conservative lifestyle soon puts them at odds with their progressive neighbors, and they find themselves in a custody battle after child abuse allegations surface, setting up a complicated debate between two opposing cultures and worldviews.

Cristian Mungiu’s latest film is based on a real-life court case.

Recent findings suggest that the film was shot over 36 days in spring 2025 in Western Norway’s Hjørundfjorden. The dramatic and mostly tourist-free fjord near the city of Ålesund cuts through the Sunnmøre Alps, with peaks rising up to 5,600 feet directly from the water.

For the family home, location scouts selected a tiny village called Stenes, comprising just a few rustic buildings scattered on the shores of the fjord’s Norangsfjorden arm. Nearby, they shot church scenes at a simple wooden structure in the town of Øye with school scenes taking place in Sæbø and courthouse scenes being filmed in the “substantial city” of Ålesund.

As the title of the film suggests, the fjord is more than just a mere setting—it’s a poetic space suffused with symbolic meaning for Mungiu. “I was attracted by this idea of a very secluded community where people can’t avoid finally talking to one another,” Mungiu notes. “The fjord evokes for me this need for solidarity among people when confronted with extreme coldness and severe weather.”.

Mungiu sought to balance the epic scale of the fjord setting with the legal drama of the film.

In a recent development, while audiences might expect the grandeur of a fjord to humble the people who live within it, in this movie, Mungiu instead uses the geographical formation to highlight their folly. “Normally, in front of nature’s force, people should become conscious of their fragility,” Mungiu states, “but too often their huge egos make them forget how mortal and insignificant they are, and they end up investing all their energy into imposing their point of view on others.”.

It has been revealed that the landscape worked particularly well within the context of Mungiu’s unique visual storytelling style: He conceives of each scene as a single shot, without cuts or close-ups, letting his characters move through expansive frames. As he describes it, “Every shot needs to be perfectly balanced in terms of light, interpretation, choreography, rhythm.” For this project, he imagined scenes that would call to mind the winter landscapes of Flemish Renaissance master Pieter Bruegel the Elder, who painted small human figures dwarfed by snowy scenery. The wide shots, Mungiu says, “allow the majestic nature to feel a bit intimidating and menacing.”.

The winter landscapes in the film were inspired by the work of Flemish Renaissance painter Pieter Bruegel the Elder.

When it came time to select the perfect fjord, Mungiu was purely pragmatic. “I imagine scenes quite in detail when I write the screenplay and while scouting,” he explains. “I try to find locations as close as possible to what I’ve imagined.” He drew a “very precise sketch” for his location scout of what he was looking for: two neighboring houses at the end of a fjord, “with mountains and forests behind, quiet deep water in front, and a narrow road connecting them to the rest of the world—all this ideally covered in snow during wintertime.”.

His production team found a spot that looked just as he envisioned in Stenes, deep down the fjord and away from the coast, to maximize the potential for more snow. Then the hardest part started: convincing the homeowners to rent their properties out for the shoot.

Sources indicate that “Once we started our scouting, we felt that we were visiting a form of paradise,” he says. “The light always comes from an angle, the air is pure, the colors are strong, the calm of the ocean is threatening, the snow on the peaks looks menacing.” Everything in the area, he continues, “is clean, organized, precise, logical, and functional.” Mungiu jokes, “For an OCD person like me, it was the perfect place.”.

Of course, the wildness of the fjord came with its own set of challenges, from avalanche warnings to a lack of consistent snow cover (they trucked in powder from the mountains). But Mungiu and his team tried to use these problems to their artistic advantage. On the first day of shooting, for instance, a major storm forced them to move production inside and shoot an emotionally complex scene. Inspired by the dramatic gusts, they hung an enormous Norwegian flag just outside the window to thrash and snap in the gale, “adding a visual element to the inner feelings of Lisbet in a very delicate moment for her as a character.”.

In a recent development, the primary gateway town for the fjord is Ålesund, a coastal city known for its abundant Art Nouveau architecture. While it’s only about 20 miles from Stenes as the crow flies, the journey takes about two hours of scenic driving and ferry crossings to get to the spots where the movie was shot.

Sebastian Stan as Mihai Gheorghiu, the devout evangelical main character who relocates his family to the titular Norwegian fjord.

Sources indicate that if you want to see the fjord for yourself, an ideal lodging option is the lovely Hotel Union Øye, which opened early for the season to host the cast. Now a member of Relais & Châteaux, the gingerbread-like hotel debuted in 1891 and over the decades has hosted the likes of Henrik Ibsen, Arthur Conan Doyle, and Edvard Grieg, who composed music on the piano in the salon.

According to recent reports, it’s also possible to visit Hjørundfjorden on one of Norway’s most iconic journeys: a sailing with Hurtigruten, which is part pleasure cruise line, part local passenger ferry, and part cargo vessel for remote communities. In 2027, the line’s Coastal Express route, which hugs the coast from Bergen in the south to Kirkenes in the north, will visit Hjørundfjorden in May and September, while the Svalbard Line will make a stop at Sæbø in the fjord from May through September. (In the film’s Ålesund-set courtroom scenes, you can even see the ferry looming outside the windows.).

Havila Voyages, a family-run Hurtigruten competitor, also stops in Hjørundfjorden seasonally from September 1 to October 31; optional excursions include a scenic drive through the surrounding countryside and mountain valleys; an e-bike tour through the narrow Norangsdalen valley along the “Queen’s Route” (so named because it was supposedly visited by seven queens); or a guided hike to a mountain dairy farm, followed by a snack of a svele (crepe).

In a recent development, and if you can’t make it to Norway, Mungiu is presenting an exhibition of his photographs from scouting trips and the film’s production called Fjord. The Pictures at Newly introduced York’s Romanian Cultural Institute in New York (through November 30). His images, all shot on a phone, depict the landscapes, people, architecture, and even weather that helped shape the film’s visual language.

P&O Cruises has declared that it has placed regional choices at the heart of its Caribbean fly-cruise program, offering more than half of its charter flights for winter 2026-27 departing from airports outside London.

Carnival UK and P&O Cruises President Paul Ludlow mentioned: “A Caribbean holiday should feel effortless from the moment it begins and for many of our guests that means being able to start their journey closer to home.”.

“We have increased availability from Scotland, Belfast, Cardiff and Newcastle, as well as introducing Exeter, and regional flight availability will continue to be an notable area of growth for us in the years ahead,” added Ludlow.

The firm said in a press release that its program features 14-night sailings with flights included, allowing guests to start their Caribbean adventure from airports across the UK.

Manchester, Birmingham and London departures make up the majority of the program, with flights available for all 14-night Barbados roundtrip itineraries.

Manchester alone represents approximately half of all P&O Cruises non-London charter flights to the Caribbean.

The organization mentioned that regional choice is also continuing to grow, with Scottish airports seeing the largest year-on-year increase in available departures for winter 2026-27, with charter availability growing by approximately a third, primarily from Edinburgh.

P&O Cruises has also increased availability from Belfast, Cardiff and Newcastle, while Exeter has been introduced as a upcoming departure airport.

Guests also benefit from direct flights to the Caribbean.

P&O Cruises guests can also check in their luggage at their UK departure airport and have it delivered directly to their cabin onboard.

From November 2027, the Arvia and Iona will sail Caribbean itineraries starting and ending in St Kitts, with the island’s capital, Basseterre, becoming an additional turnaround port for Iona’s fly-cruise program.

P&O Cruises added that it has released a Black Friday sale, offering savings of up to £500 per cabin on holidays alongside a Black Friday Price Drop Guarantee.

Available until midnight on December 1, 2026, the promotion applies to selected holidays booked on Select Price or Early Saver fares, departing between March 6, 2027, and October 28, 2028.

The sale covers holidays including the Caribbean, Norwegian fjords and the Mediterranean.

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., flanked by House Minority Whip Katherine M.
  • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries won a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday setting him up to be the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, a historic step that follows Democrats’ staggering election wins earlier this month.
  • It has been revealed that jeffries, who had called for a recorded vote of the more than 250-member caucus that will serve in the next Congress despite facing no revealed opponent, won decisively, 251-11.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., flanked by House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., and House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., hold a press conference in the Capitol after the House Democratic leadership elections on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries won a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday setting him up to be the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, a historic step that follows Democrats’ staggering election wins earlier this month.

It has been revealed that jeffries, who had called for a recorded vote of the more than 250-member caucus that will serve in the next Congress despite facing no revealed opponent, won decisively, 251-11. The margin suggests Jeffries will easily surpass the necessary 218 votes he will need on the House floor when the full chamber votes in January.

“It's a high honor and a distinct privilege to stand before the American people today as a Democratic nominee to be the next Speaker of the United States House of Representatives,” Jeffries said at a press conference following the election.

According to recent reports, while Jeffries celebrates his win, he has continued to put an emphasis on unity before he faces what has been deemed the toughest job in Washington. Democrats’ massive majority will give him some margin for maneuvering as he balances the priorities of a complex caucus ranging from moderates to progressives.

Recent findings suggest that “Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other,” Jeffries responded when asked about the 11 defections and what they mean for the next Congress. “Fight MAGA extremism, and to get big things done for the American people, and that is what we are going to accomplish together, beginning on January 3rd.”.

Seven of the 11 members who intended to vote against Jeffries released a statement saying that conversations with leadership are still “ongoing” and that there is “work to be done,” but noting there has been “meaningful progress.” The seven included Reps.- elect Darializa Avilia Chavelier, D-N.Y., Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., Frederick Haynes, D-Texas, Melat Kiros, D-Colo., Donovan McKinney, D-Mich., Chris Rabb, D-Pa., and Claire Valdez, D-N.Y.

“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these concerns,” they wrote. “We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations.”.

Newly elected House Democrats will meet with former President Barack Obama Wednesday night, where party unity will also be a likely topic.

It has been revealed that “This is the beginning of a new bargain, a new politics where hard work is honored and where people's voice is paramount, and where we have more confidence in the future than nostalgia for the past,” House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., said at the press conference.

Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., who made history two decades ago as the nation’s first female speaker, arrived for the vote chanting “Hakeem Jeffries!”, reflecting party leaders’ desire to start the long morning of balloting on a positive note.

Recent findings suggest that jeffries' nomination followed the election of current Democratic Caucus Vice Chairman Ted Lieu, D-Calif., to serve as the caucus chair in the next Congress. Separate votes followed Wednesday morning, keeping Jeffries' leadership team intact: Clark, as the upcoming majority leader and Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., as majority whip.

At his news conference, Jeffries noted that Clark was also making history as the first woman ever to serve in the position. Aguilar will also be the first Latino to serve as majority whip.

In a recent development, “We've been looking at people's talents, not a particular gender or race, and I think that's a good thing,” outgoing Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, D-Md., a former majority leader, told reporters ahead of the election.

Sources indicate that “I think Hakeem Jeffries is going to be a good speaker,” Hoyer continued. “He has the confidence of the caucus, and he has a good leadership team that is close knit and very organized.”.

Jeffries expressed confidence in the weeks leading up to his securing the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who had noted they remained “undecided” ahead of the election.

Pelosi was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to move forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

Sources indicate that the entire leadership team will be tested despite their numerical advantage over Republicans by the same internal tensions facing Senate Democrats, where current Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., is being challenged for leadership of the majority by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md.

Jeffries remarked Tuesday that the approach to the caucus vote mirrored the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who was best positioned to lead based on their “track record, experience and vision.”.

Jeffries has already outlined some of his top priorities of his speakership such as a hefty healthcare agenda, immigration legislation, and a multitude of investigations into the Trump administration.

He also signaled Wednesday another area where his party’s restive base is likely to close ranks: oversight.

“House Democrats will hold the crooks accountable, not for partisan reasons, but for patriotic ones,” he noted at his news conference.

  • The façades of the houses on Bad Tölz’s Marktstraße glow with festive lights in the evening.
  • According to recent reports, in Bavaria’s Bad Tölz, a medieval town sitting on the Isar River, the scent of roasted almonds mingles with the sound of Christmas carols, while the historic market square is decorated with garlands and wreaths.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You don’t have to travel to Munich or Nuremberg to get into the Christmas spirit and enjoy some lebkuchen or pfeffernüsse. The streets of the country’s small towns are also filled with holiday cheer that’s best experienced at their Christmas markets. Amid their narrow alleys and on cobblestone squares, there’s a special atmosphere every December. Here’s our selection of seven to visit this season.

The façades of the houses on Bad Tölz’s Marktstraße glow with festive lights in the evening.

According to recent reports, in Bavaria’s Bad Tölz, a medieval town sitting on the Isar River, the scent of roasted almonds mingles with the sound of Christmas carols, while the historic market square is decorated with garlands and wreaths. At the Christmas market, approximately 40 festively decorated stalls are set up right in front of the historic façades of the old town. The atmosphere is especially magical in the evening hours when the Christmas lights sparkle everywhere. For children, there’s a carousel, a curated program of activities, and the popular Family Wednesdays with discounts and carriage rides.

In a recent development, hours: 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. daily, from November 27 to December 23, 2026; 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. on December 24.

The Wernigerode Christmas Market is set against the backdrop of some of the historic buildings in this town in the Harz Mountains. Snow often covers the roofs, and Christmas carols fill the air at the popular event.

Hours: Sunday to Thursday, 11 a.m. to 8 p.m.; Friday and Saturday, 11 a.m. to 9 p.m.; from November 20 to December 22, 2026.

The medieval town of Rothenburg ob der Tauber is even more magical than usual during the Christmas season.

Industry observers note that in the pre-Christmas season, the medieval town of Rothenburg ob der Tauber, located on the Romantic Road in Bavaria, becomes even more enchanting. The opening of the market is a small spectacle when, on the Friday before the first Sunday of Advent, the large Christmas tree on the market square is illuminated in a festive ceremony. The town’s Christmas market continues a tradition with more than 500 years of history. In the narrow alleys and squares near the town hall, including the market square, visitors will find everything they could desire as they embrace the Christmas season: from gifts like handmade jewelry to freshly baked gingerbread. The Christmas Village, a nearly 11,000-square-foot store located not far from the Market Square, continues the holiday spirit year-round.

Hours: Sunday to Thursday, 11 a.m. to 7 p.m.; Fridays and Saturdays, 11 a.m. to 8 p.m.; from November 20 to December 23, 2026, closed November 23.

A special feature of the Gengenbach Advent Market is the window-opening ritual which transforms the town hall into an enormous advent calendar.

Recent findings suggest that one of the things that makes the Gengenbach Advent Market in the Black Forest stand out is its window-opening ritual. On December 1, the town hall transforms into the world’s largest Advent calendar with a unique art display. Every evening at 6 p.m., one of 24 windows opens. In each one there’s a work of art, often by world-renowned artists such as Marc Chagall and Andy Warhol. Visitors from all over the world come to Gengenbach to see this unique calendar against the romantic backdrop of the historic old town.

Sources indicate that hours: Monday to Friday, 2 p.m. to 8 p.m.; Saturdays and Sundays, 11:30 a.m. to 8 p.m. From November 27 to December 23, 2026.

Quedlinburg is already a World Heritage City, but during the Christmas season it becomes even more romantic.

It has been revealed that hours: Sunday to Thursday, 11 a.m. to 8 p.m.; Fridays, 11 a.m. to 10 p.m.; Saturdays, 10 a.m. to 10 p.m.. From November 25 to December 22, 2026.

An enchanting setting and a varied program are the draws at the Bernkastel-Kues Christmas Market.

In a recent development, A torch-lit swim, fireworks, and a hike with St. Nicholas: During Advent, the Christmas market in Bernkastel-Kues, a town in a famous winegrowing town near the borders with Luxembourg and Belgium, offers a program of activities that few can match. Torch-lit swimmers bravely plunge into the cold, wintry Moselle on December 5, and both children and adults can join St. Nicholas on a hike on December 6. (The route varies each year, but it always begins at the market square and typically covers between six and nine miles.) This year marks the 48th time the historic old town has served as the backdrop for this romantic Christmas market. Amid half-timbered façades and cobblestone streets, stalls offer traditional crafts, gift ideas, and delicious treats.

In a recent development, hours: Sunday to Thursday, 11 a.m. to 7 p.m.; Fridays and Saturdays, 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. From November 20 to December 20, 2026, closed November 22.

Small and charming, but also very brief: The Meersburg Christmas Market is open for only two days.

Admittedly, a weekend isn’t much time to experience the Christmas market in the old town of Meersburg, on the shores of Lake Constance (Bodensee) in southwestern Germany. But with some carefully planning, you can make the most of the time you have. Both days are packed with Christmas activities, ranging from barrel organ music to readings and puppet shows for the youngest visitors. The stalls sell handicrafts, regional products, and Christmas treats. The market in the castle park is a highlight. And because the event is so short, it makes it all the more special with all the holiday fun concentrated in just two days.

According to recent reports, hours: 3 p.m. to 9 p.m., Friday, November 27, and 2 p.m. to 8 p.m., Saturday, November 28, 2026.

This article was originally published on Condé Nast Traveller Germany.

Transcend Cruises has launched a partnership with Your Health Companion (YHC) to introduce a personal health benefit designed to enhance the well-being, confidence and peace of mind of its charter river cruise guests.

“At Transcend Cruises, we are continually looking for innovative ways to elevate the guest experience. Our partnership with Your Health Companion reflects our commitment to providing guests not only with extraordinary travel experiences but also with greater confidence and peace of mind while exploring the world,” said Edie Rodriguez, CEO, Transcend Cruises.

Through this partnership, Transcend Cruises guests will receive complimentary seven-day access to Your Health Companion, a personal health management app that puts essential medical information, health resources and AI-powered symptom guidance directly at their fingertips.

“We believe that traveling away from home should never mean being disconnected from your personal health information,” noted Scott Grody, CEO, Your Health Companion.

Industry observers note that “Our partnership with Transcend Cruises represents an exciting advancement in bringing personalized health technology to the travel industry. We are providing travelers with many of the benefits of having their doctor’s office in their pocket, wherever their journey takes them,” added Grody.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in the late 1800s, travelers arriving on the West Coast found that the gold rush had dried up, but another kind of treasure was waiting in its wake: the health spa. Soon, doctors back east were prescribing trips to the Golden State for ailing patients in search of restorative sunshine, mineral springs, and fresh air. California’s reputation as a destination for serious R&R has persisted ever since. From beachfront properties in SoCal to redwood hideaways along the Big Sur coast to vineyardside estates in Napa Valley, the best resorts in California are a kind of gold standard all their own.

Recent findings suggest that of course, it’s a big state with hundreds of different landscapes, so finding the right resort is all about knowing what makes you come alive. Looking to spend time on the links? There are legendary fairways waiting at Pebble Beach. Craving an off-the-grid escape? Decamp to a secluded sanctuary in the Santa Rosa Mountains. Prefer five-star amenities with near-clairvoyant service, or a home base for wine tastings and lavish dining? Consider it covered. Read on for the best resorts in California, where the good life is the real gold rush.

Auberge Collection’s third property in Napa Valley is set on a historic Wine Country ranch founded in 1856 by Judge Edward Stanly. Guests can choose from 135 cottages, rooms, and suites—decorated in oatmeal and beige hues with leather and oak furnishings—all with private terraces and outdoor showers. Standout amenities include Guatemalan heated robes, yoga mats, and Theragun massage tools. Bay Area food lovers make the trek here just to sample chef Anthony Stagnaro’s ingredient-focused meals at the resort’s Avroko-designed restaurant, Bear; others prefer to sip rosé at the French countryside-inspired Basin Bar or order a scoop of ice cream at The Window. But don’t expect to drink wine all day: This wellness-focused resort can curate fitness optimization programs, send you out on a cycling adventure with a pro, or arrange a hot-air balloon ride for the whole family. —Jen Murphy.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

While it’s tempting to paint Sonoma as a sleepy sweep of California Wine Country, the truth is, the county is every bit as—if not more—booming than neighboring Napa. It’s got Michelin-starred restaurants, shiny new tasting rooms, and substantial-name hotels cropping up on the regular. But to try a little of that sweet Sonoma of yesteryear, there’s no better place than Farmhouse Inn. Located near the Russian River—and within easy driving distance to charming Healdsburg, as well as some of the region's best vineyards—this 25-room property feels delightfully laid-back and intimate. The Inn has five different room categories, all with a country-chic look; bright and airy with white wainscoting, pillowy bedding, and haute-rustic touches that might include a personal welcome message on a small blackboard, a fireplace, and comfortable overstuffed chairs. The Farmhouse Restaurant occupies a beautiful space and offers an ever-evolving chef’s tasting menu with hyper-local ingredients paired with, naturally, a stellar regional wine list. All in all, Farmhouse Inn looks and feels like a classic New England country charmer—with California Wine Country street cred. —Rebecca Misner.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

This outstanding Napa Valley hotel is set on 33 acres of vineyards and olive groves—needless to say, the views are spectacular. Sumptuous cottages done in sun and earth tones have wood-burning fireplaces and refrigerators stocked with local wines and cheeses; bathrooms come with skylights and flat-screen TVs. The restaurant serves Wine Country cuisine with French and Mediterranean influences, and its terrace has heaters for dining out on cool evenings. Enjoy Italian ices and chilled towels at the pool and Reiki at La Pagode, an Asian-style pavilion. —Todd Plummer.

Napa has a handful of excellent hotels and no shortage of fabulous wineries and tasting rooms, but this is the first full-on luxury resort that marries the two. The property’s 85 rooms and suites, as well as 20 private residences, are surrounded by acres of vineyards. The bar and dining space are gorgeous—soaring ceilings, a glassed-in kitchen, and a wall of glass doors that open onto a huge terrace with a firepit—but made cozy by comfy booths and warm lighting. The on-site winery and its tasting room are another way this resort stands out. It’s a dream to walk from your room to a tasting and not have to worry about driving or calling a car. —R.M.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

Northern California’s Wine Country retreats often model themselves on faraway places; destinations with longer traditions and more old-world gravitas. This is too bad, because their location, between the Pacific and the Mayacamas Mountains, is pure magic, and by this point on the domestic wine timeline, there’s no need to apologize for who you are. This is why the arrival of Montage’s first property in the region, and Sonoma’s first large-scale luxury resort, was so exciting when it opened in 2020. It celebrates its own landscape, leaving the 22,000 live oaks in place and pulling a palette of dun and moss from the surrounding sun-soaked vineyards. The restaurant offers a bounty of Sonoma’s best, with everything—from the Pliny the Elder IPA to the lamb shank—sourced from within miles. And the local sixth-generation vintners who frequent the sprawling patio bar are happy to remind you that there is, in fact, plenty of history in these parts. —R.M.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

There are golf resorts, and then there’s Casa Palmero at Pebble Beach. The course, Pebble Beach Golf Links, opened more than 100 years ago in 1919, and has enjoyed as long and storied a history as any. The resort, a former private residence that opened in 1999, is directly on the course—rooms overlook the first and second fairways—making it an absolute dream for golfers. But Casa Palmero offers so much more than tee times. The rooms have a countryside vibe—spacious with wood-burning fireplaces, exposed ceiling beams, and wrought-iron fixtures—while the Spa at Pebble Beach offers award-winning service. Plus, it’s only a five-minute walk down to the peaceful beach.

Recent findings suggest that set on 500 acres in the foothills of the Santa Lucia Mountains along California’s Central Coast, Carmel Valley Ranch is located just shy of 13 miles from the Monterey Bay Aquarium and historic Cannery Row. At check-in, you’ll receive a list of the resort’s scheduled activities, and staff will likely share their favorites—and you should pay attention. Options range from guided hikes and yoga to archery lessons and picnics with Pablo and Paco, a pair of resident miniature donkeys. There are also multiple pools, tennis and pickleball courts, and an 18-hole Pete Dye–designed golf course. If the blinds are up at the on-site creamery, stopping by the window to watch the cheesemaker in action is a must. Along with chickens and a salt house, the organic garden is home to veggies, flowers, and honeybees. Menus at signature restaurant Valley Kitchen showcase fresh, local ingredients—many of which are grown or produced on the resort. —Dana Rebmann.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

It has been revealed that this beloved Big Sur resort, which dramatically overlooks the Pacific and is surrounded by acres of forest, received a total reboot in 2025. And while it may look fresh—rooms have all been updated with plenty of wood and neutrals, 15 luxe safari-style tents have been added to the roster, and the spa got a relaxation deck that looks out at the ocean—it hasn't lost its laid-back 1970s vibe. It's still, hands down, one of the most magical places to disconnect and get back in touch with nature. —Christina Ohly Evans.

The Post Ranch Inn is a total immersion in the singular landscape of Big Sur, in environs defined by a sense of understated luxury. The Ranch’s 40 rooms have all been designed to both blend in with and have a light touch upon the land, and range from tree houses to clifftop suites with expansive views of the mountains to the east or, better yet, the ocean’s expanse to the west. Engage with the environment some more by exploring the property’s hiking trails, taking a tour of the chef’s garden, or signing up for a falconry lesson. —Lauren Sloss.

Check Availability at Hotels.com.

According to recent reports, it might seem like a mistake to go to Santa Barbara and not stay close to the shore, but the moment you make the turn inland onto San Ysidro Road, you realize that being here isn’t about visiting Santa Barbara; it’s about visiting the ranch. Just 38 cottages, each with its own unique layout, decor, and view, are spread out over 550 acres, but rather than being scattered, they form a ring within the property. At the resort’s center is a collection of gardens as well as a rectangular pool that overlooks the canyon. Some of the curated finds you’ll see throughout are museum-quality art, antiques sourced from the owner’s world travels, and handmade wallpapers. But San Ysidro Ranch isn’t your typical hotel—as its history of having legendary guests like Jacqueline and John F. Kennedy, who honeymooned here, or John Huston, who finished writing the screenplay for The African Queen on the property, can attest. It continues its legacy as a celebrity refuge, as modern-day A-listers use this tucked-away spot to truly hide out and escape—which is what you should do too. —Samantha Brooks.

This is the original Hollywood hideaway with seven acres of land nestled in the foothills of the American Riviera. At El Encanto, you’ll have views overlooking the Pacific Coast with the rose-colored mountains rising behind you. The property has 90 rooms, but it never feels crowded; in fact, it feels private and idyllic. It has a fantastic luxe Spanish colonial charm without being annoying or precious. Whether you’re hiding away in a lush garden suite with a fireplace and a patio or just swanning around on the terrace for an alfresco farmers market lunch, it feels just right: low-key but ultra stylish. Call it what it is: a retreat. —Daniel Scheffler.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

Arriving at Rosewood Miramar Beach, with its military-straight rows of white roses and pristine clapboard cottages, feels like landing on a postcard-perfect street in Cape Cod. If it all seems a little too perfect, well, there was time to get things right. The former Miramar by the Sea Hotel occupied these 16 oceanfront acres from 1889 until it closed for renovations in 2000. The hotel sat half-demolished for years, its second act tangled in red tape. It took SoCal billionaire developer Rick Caruso and the Hong Kong–based Rosewood Hotel Group to push the project through. And while it may have been tempting to scrap the past after such a treacherous road to reopening, the latest Miramar deliberately throws back. Lemon-yellow-and-white striped umbrellas flank a rectangular pool where the Scoop Shop serves up fountain drinks, ice cream cones, and burgers. Overlooking the ocean, there’s Caruso’s, the type of place where you order a martini with your cacio e pepe alongside a heaping dollop of la dolce vita (the chef hails from Harry’s Bar in Rome)—and, in a state where “formal flip-flops" are a thing, one that blessedly enforces a dress code. In case you start to feel too lost in the 1950s, an outpost from Malibu Farm and a Goop boutique remind you that this is indeed modern-day Cali. —R.M.

Check Availability at Hotels.com.

Time slows down as you drive down the oversized, oak-tree-lined driveway at Alisal Ranch. Immediately upon checking in, you're greeted with countryside hospitality that makes you feel like you're light-years away from LA. The rooms are furnished with just the right amount of country Western kitsch, complete with wood-burning fireplaces, Pendleton blankets, and vintage paintings, and the beds are incredibly comfy—the perfect spot to rest your head after a day of adventuring. The highlight of your weekend will undoubtedly be horseback riding through groves of oaks up to the pancake breakfast. And the bar deserves a nod too, with a giant fireplace that makes for the perfect spot to enjoy a whiskey neat. —K.S.

In a recent development, to book a stay at this impeccably designed escape, guests must send an inquiry through the website—a sign of just how exclusive the hotel is. The reward is an extremely private getaway with a relaxing, neutral design and an incredible Nobu restaurant. Opened in April 2017, this serene escape was once a 1950s-era beach motel. Now, it's a study in high-design restraint—which is clear after setting one foot inside its almost hidden entrance. Guests enter through a courtyard that looks out onto the ocean, which leads to a beautiful garden. Follow the path to a deck made from ipe wood that overlooks Carbon Beach and Malibu Pier. —Brooke Porter Katz.

Industry observers note that montage Laguna Beach is a polished, residential-style resort set on 30 oceanfront acres along one of Southern California’s most scenic stretches of coastline. Opened in 2003 as the brand’s flagship, the hotel continues to deliver consistent high-level service, a strong food and beverage program, and a true sense of privacy despite its size. Every one of the 263 rooms has an ocean view and outdoor space, and the property's layout, from the cliffside paths, tiered lawns, and access to Treasure Island Beach, makes it easy to settle in and stay awhile. Guests skew toward special-occasion travelers, West Coast couples, families, and loyal Montage regulars who return year after year. Highlights include the 20,000-square-foot Spa Montage, the renovated Mosaic Pool, direct beach access, and the return of Studio Mediterranean, the resort’s stellar fine-dining venue. While there’s no tennis or golf on-site, the concierge can arrange access at a nearby club. —Michelle Gross.

Recent findings suggest that time seems to slow down as you pull up to this sprawling Spanish revival hotel. Birds chirp from atop the towering oak trees, and the peaceful running fountains set the tone for a zen-like serenity that'll carry through your weekend. The rooms are personal retreats, many with soaking tubs, hand-painted Spanish tile, gold-auburn granite, and cobalt blue accents that give a modern Mediterranean look. Some rooms even have stucco fireplaces with seating, the perfect spot to tuck into a book and indulge in the rejuvenating spirit of Ojai. If that's not enough for you, the pools here are worth the visit alone—attentive staff, killer views, and plenty of space to hop around to keep the scenery fresh. —Krista Simmons.

Toeing the line between self-improvement sabbatical and bona fide vacation, Sensei Porcupine Creek is the ideal getaway for the chronic over-achiever: a place where real R&R is achieved proactively, through science and strategy, and in utter seclusion. Formerly the private estate of tech wizard and Silicon Valley billionaire Larry Ellison, Sensei’s co-founder, this intensely isolated retreat hidden in the foothills of the Santa Rosa Mountains is the second outpost for Sensei, and it marked the brand’s debut in the continental United States. (Its first, Sensei Lānaʻi, A Four Seasons Resort, opened in 2019.) But it’s also the brand’s first true standalone property, and with a lush, 75-acre golf course, a glamorous lagoon-style pool, and tennis facilities modeled after those at the nearby Indian Wells Tennis Garden—which hosts the annual BNP Paribas Tennis Tournament—it really does stand alone. —Betsy Blumenthal.

Industry observers note that the Resort at Pelican Hill, located in the ultra-exclusive Newport Coast zip code, has a luxurious Tuscan vibe, with well-manicured hills overlooking the Pacific, beautiful villas and bungalows, and Roman aqueduct–style architecture. At 504 acres, it's huge—so huge that you'll likely need your car to get to your room. It's also surrounded by 50,000 acres of protected green spaces. You'll want to leave plenty of time to relax by the Coliseum Pool, the resort's crown jewel. —Archana Ram.

This sprawling getaway is peak California. Think orange groves, bright pink bougainvillea, and Spanish Colonial architecture. The main features—the suites, restaurants, lobby—are spread out across 45 acres, making it feel more like a luxurious neighborhood than a typical resort. Located in Rancho Santa Fe, a ritzy enclave 25 miles north of downtown San Diego, this place has the whole package—beautiful decor, dedicated service, next-level amenities, well-manicured grounds, and a serene vibe. —Jennie Nunn.

Check Availability at Mr and Mrs Smith.

What is the best luxury resort in California?

Recent findings suggest that san Ysidro Ranch, at the foot of the Santa Ynez Mountains, is one of the best resorts in the world, let alone California. The property sprawls across 550 acres of citrus groves, gardens, and hiking trails, and each of its 38 rooms is a luxury cottage with a stone fireplace and antique furnishings that reflect its 130+ year history. Dignitaries like Winston Churchill, Audrey Hepburn, and Lucille Ball have stayed here—not to mention JFK and Jackie Kennedy, who called it their honeymoon hotel in 1953.

What is the best place to visit in California if you're a first-time visitor?

In a recent development, california is so varied that it’s hard to pick a favorite zone, but there are few places in the world like Significant Sur, where redwoods tower overhead and dramatic cliffs drop to the Pacific below. It can be a bit rustic, but that’s a big part of the charm.

What is the difference between a hotel and resort?

Sources indicate that A hotel is mainly a place to sleep. A resort is the destination itself. Resorts typically sit on larger grounds and bundle the amenities you’d otherwise have to leave to find, like spas, pools, golf, multiple restaurants, and organized activities, so you can spend your whole stay on-property. In California, that might mean a round of golf at Pebble Beach before dinner, or a day of hiking, a massage, and a wine tasting without needing to hop in your car.

How we choose the best resorts in California.

In a recent development, every hotel review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind.

Dems express ‘points of anxiety’ over Trump’s summit with Putin and Xi
